# Overview



This page is the entry point to the OpenPhase repository. It explains what OpenPhase is, what problems it solves, how the codebase is organized into a dataset, benchmark tasks, generative models, and an interactive explorer — and it gives you a guided reading path into the rest of this documentation. No prior knowledge of Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation or this codebase is assumed; every concept introduced here is expanded in later catalog pages.

## What Is OpenPhase?

**OpenPhase** is an open-source platform and dataset for studying **Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation (LLPS)** — the process by which biomolecules (proteins, RNA, DNA) condense into droplet-like phases inside and outside cells. Its distinguishing claim is being the **first condition-aware platform** for system-level exploration: instead of treating phase behavior as a property of a protein sequence alone, OpenPhase treats every experiment as a tuple of *components* (the protein, optionally a nucleic acid) and *environmental conditions* (pH, salt, temperature, crowders, concentrations) together with a measured outcome.

![OpenPhase banner](https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase/blob/main/assets/openphase-main.webp?raw=true)

Why does the condition-aware framing matter? A protein like FUS may phase-separate at pH 6 with 150 mM NaCl but stay dissolved at pH 8 with 1 M salt. A dataset that collapses all of those experiments into one binary "this protein is a phase-separating protein" label throws away exactly the information experimentalists need. OpenPhase keeps every condition of every experiment as a separate record, which enables three canonical tasks defined in the repository:

1. **Phase outcome prediction** — given components (x) and conditions (c), predict whether the system undergoes LLPS (y ∈ {0, 1}).
2. **Condition inference** — given components and an outcome, infer the conditions that produce it, enabling rational experimental design.
3. **Phase system design** — generate protein sequences (x) that exhibit desired phase behavior under target conditions, using generative models.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L14), [README.md](README.md#L56-L67), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L3-L4)

## The Three Pillars: Dataset, Benchmarks and Models, and the Explorer

OpenPhase is best understood as three cooperating layers, each visible in the repository root:

![Single-protein systems](https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase/blob/main/assets/fig-protein1-systems.webp?raw=true)

![Multi-protein systems](https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase/blob/main/assets/fig-multi-protein-systems.webp?raw=true)

**Pillar 1 — the condition-level dataset.** The `data/` folder holds one `records.tsv` table per *system*, where a **system** is the set of an experiment's components without concentrations (protein-only, protein + RNA, protein + DNA, or protein with a measured saturation concentration). A thin API in `openphase_systems.py` — `list_systems()`, `load_system()`, `load_all()` — loads these tables as pandas DataFrames, with optional filtering by source. In total the four systems hold **11,439 records** merged and de-duplicated from LLPSDB v2, LLPSense, RNAPSEC, a PhaSepDB 3 pilot extraction, Bremer 2022 and Ausserwöger 2025.

| System | What it contains | Records | Folder |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `protein` | protein only | 7,490 | `data/protein/` |
| `protein_RNA` | protein + RNA | 2,511 | `data/protein_RNA/` |
| `protein_DNA` | protein + DNA | 662 | `data/protein_DNA/` |
| `protein_csat` | protein, saturation concentration (a measured value, no binary label) | 776 | `data/protein_csat/` |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L32-L41), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L6-L14), [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L1-L11), [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L28-L46), [README.md](README.md#L43-L47)

**Pillar 2 — benchmarks and generative models.** The task scripts formalize the canonical tasks: `task1.py` runs **outcome-prediction baselines** (an AdaBoost classifier tuned with Optuna and evaluated with AUROC/AUPRC/kappa/MCC, plus a Droppler-style self-attention neural baseline), while `task2.py` trains **PhaseCVAE**, a Conditional Variational Autoencoder for condition inference and phase-diagram prediction on protein-RNA systems. The generative side lives in two model packages: `Discrete/` (a discrete diffusion model over amino-acid sequences, built around `DiscreteMarginalTransition` and ESM2 embeddings) and `ldm/` (a latent diffusion pipeline with a conditional UNet denoiser and classifier-free guidance). All of these consume sequences and conditions through a unified embedding layer configured by `meta_config.py` and produced by `meta_embed.py`.

Sources: [task1.py](task1.py#L59-L104), [task1.py](task1.py#L143-L176), [task2.py](task2.py#L1-L4), [Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py](Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L1-L12), [ldm/training.py](ldm/training.py#L4-L27)

**Pillar 3 — the records space explorer.** The `records_space/` folder builds and hosts an entirely browser-based interactive map of all 11,439 single-protein records, published via GitHub Pages. Each dot is one experiment; the layout is a t-SNE of a weighted distance combining protein similarity (ESMC-600M embeddings), nucleic-acid properties, experimental conditions, and buffer/additive families. A companion page shows **35,107 negative and unlabelled proteins** (the training negatives of ten LLPS-prediction tools against a Swiss-Prot reference sample). You can filter, colour, and deep-link into specific systems or sources directly from a URL.

| Distance block | Weight | Content |
|---|---:|---|
| protein | 0.40 | ESMC-600M layer-18 embedding (z-score, PCA to 64 dims, cosine) |
| conditions | 0.35 | protein concentration, pH, temperature, salts, crowders |
| nucleic acid | 0.15 | present/absent, RNA/DNA class, length, concentration, fold features |
| buffer and additives | 0.10 | buffer family and additive families |

Sources: [records_space/README.md](records_space/README.md#L1-L4), [records_space/README.md](records_space/README.md#L11-L20), [records_space/README.md](records_space/README.md#L52-L58)

> [!TIP]
> Unreported values are **never imputed** anywhere in OpenPhase. In the record tables a missing condition is left empty and flagged by a paired `st_*` state column (`obs` / `miss` / `zero` / `rt`); in the explorer, a non-reported value counts as *its own state* in the distance model. If you build on this data, preserve that convention — silently filling gaps will distort both benchmarks and the map.

## Software Architecture at a Glance

The Mermaid diagram below shows how the three pillars connect. Reading guide: boxes are components (a folder, script, or table), arrows are data flow, and each `subgraph` groups one architectural layer — raw sources on the left flow rightward into records, embeddings, tasks/models, and finally the explorer.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Sources["Experimental sources"]
        S1["LLPSDB v2"]
        S2["Lab notebooks (Zhang lab)"]
        S3["RNAPSEC"]
        S4["LLPSense · PhaSepDB 3 pilot · Bremer · Ausserwöger"]
    end

    subgraph Loaders["Source loaders — zhanglab/"]
        DB1["db1.py"]
        DB2["db2.py"]
        DB3["db3.py"]
    end

    subgraph DataLayer["Condition-level records — data/"]
        REC["records.tsv per system<br/>(protein · protein_RNA · protein_DNA · protein_csat)"]
    end

    subgraph EmbedLayer["Embedding layer"]
        MC["meta_config.py<br/>3 configurable axes"]
        ME["meta_embed.py<br/>ESMC-600M · MTDP"]
    end

    subgraph TasksLayer["Benchmarks"]
        T1["task1.py<br/>outcome prediction baselines"]
        T2["task2.py<br/>PhaseCVAE condition inference"]
    end

    subgraph GenLayer["Generative models"]
        DD["Discrete/<br/>discrete diffusion"]
        LDM["ldm/<br/>latent diffusion + JTAE"]
    end

    EXP["records_space/<br/>interactive browser explorer"]

    S1 --> DB1
    S2 --> DB2
    S3 --> DB3
    DB1 --> ME
    DB2 --> ME
    DB3 --> ME
    S4 --> REC
    REC --> MC --> ME
    REC --> T1
    REC --> T2
    ME --> T1
    ME --> T2
    ME --> DD
    ME --> LDM
    REC --> EXP
```

Two distinct data paths exist, and beginners frequently confuse them. The **merged path** goes straight into `data/<system>/records.tsv` — flat, de-duplicated tables that `openphase_systems.py` loads. The **per-source path** goes through `zhanglab/db1.py`, `db2.py`, and `db3.py`, which download raw upstream data and build one *embedded* AnnData (`.h5ad`) dataset per source; these must be run from the repository root because they import `meta_config.py` and `meta_embed.py`. Notably, the laboratory-notebook records (db2) exist only on this second path — they are **not** in the `data/` tables.

Sources: [zhanglab/README.md](zhanglab/README.md#L1-L14), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L22-L26), [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L1-L11), [meta_embed.py](meta_embed.py#L1-L12)

## The Embedding System in One Table

Every model in OpenPhase consumes sequences and conditions as vectors, and *which* vectorizer to use is a first-class configuration choice. `meta_config.py` defines a `MetaEmbeddingConfig` Pydantic model with three independent axes, each validated against a fixed set of allowed methods; `create_meta_config()` is the factory the task scripts call. This design is what makes benchmark comparisons across embedding choices possible, and it is covered in depth in the Embedding System catalog section.

| Axis | Allowed values | Pydantic field default | `create_meta_config()` default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `protein_embedding` | `esmc`, `mtdp`, `rnapsec_protein`, `seq2ind`, `seq2onehot` | `esmc` | `mtdp` |
| `dna_rna_embedding` | `rnapsec_rna`, `dictionary` | `dictionary` | `dictionary` |
| `condition_embedding` | `droppler`, `rnapsec_condition`, `rnapsec_condition_class` | `droppler` | `droppler` |

Sources: [meta_config.py](meta_config.py#L6-L16), [meta_config.py](meta_config.py#L33-L41), [meta_embed.py](meta_embed.py#L38-L60)

> [!TIP]
> The two "default" columns above deliberately disagree: instantiating `MetaEmbeddingConfig()` bare gives you **ESMC** proteins, but the `create_meta_config()` factory used throughout the benchmarks defaults to **MTDP**. When reproducing baseline numbers, check which constructor a script actually calls — the protein embedding affects every downstream result.

## Repository Map

The tree below is the same structure you will browse on GitHub, annotated by pillar. The data layer is self-contained (TSV tables plus one loading module); everything else builds on it.

```
OpenPhase/
├── data/                  # [Pillar 1] records by system (protein, protein_RNA, protein_DNA, protein_csat)
├── openphase_systems.py   # [Pillar 1] list_systems / load_system / load_all API
├── zhanglab/              # [Pillar 1] archived loaders: db1 (LLPSDB v2), db2 (notebooks), db3 (RNAPSEC)
├── meta_config.py         # [Pillar 2] embedding configuration (3 axes)
├── meta_embed.py          # [Pillar 2] embedding generation (ESMC, MTDP)
├── task1.py               # [Pillar 2] outcome-prediction baselines
├── task2.py               # [Pillar 2] PhaseCVAE condition inference
├── Discrete/              # [Pillar 2] discrete diffusion model for sequences
├── ldm/                   # [Pillar 2] latent diffusion (JTAE + conditional UNet)
├── MTDP/                  # [Pillar 2] MTDP embedder
├── params_all.yaml        # global hyperparameters
├── records_space/         # [Pillar 3] explorer site, build scripts, exports, figures
├── assets/                # figures used by the README and this site
└── index.html             # GitHub Pages home page
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L69-L86), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L1-L4), [records_space/README.md](records_space/README.md#L68-L77)

# Quick Start



This page gets a beginner from a fresh clone of [OpenPhase](https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase) to working with real phase-separation data in a few minutes. You will install the repository, load condition-level experimental records as pandas DataFrames, and optionally build embedded PyTorch datasets from the three original data sources. No GPU, prior diffusion knowledge, or downloads outside the repo are required for the first path.

OpenPhase is a condition-aware platform for biomolecular Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation (LLPS): it pairs protein/nucleic-acid sequences (components, `x`) with environmental factors like salt, pH, and temperature (conditions, `c`) to explain and predict phase behavior (`y`).

![OpenPhase: from a system and its conditions to prediction, phase diagram and generation](https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase/blob/main/assets/openphase-main.webp?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L12-L16), [README.md](README.md#L1-L4)

## The Quick-Start Journey at a Glance

There are two entry points, and you can stop after either. The **records path** reads tables that ship inside the repository — nothing is downloaded, and `pandas` is the only hard dependency. The **embedded dataset path** instantiates the archived loaders in `zhanglab/`, which automatically download raw data from the original sources (LLPSDB v2, RNAPSEC), process it, and save it as AnnData (`.h5ad`) files with your chosen sequence/condition embeddings.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["git clone + cd OpenPhase"] --> B{What do you need?}
    B -->|"Inspect merged records"| C["import openphase_systems"]
    B -->|"Train models / run tasks"| D["Build embedded datasets"]
    C --> C1["list_systems()"]
    C1 --> C2["load_system / load_all"]
    C2 --> C3["pandas DataFrame"]
    D --> D1["create_meta_config(...)"]
    D1 --> D2["DB1Dataset(root='./data', ...)"]
    D2 --> D3{"Artifacts present?"}
    D3 -->|"no"| D4["auto-download raw source"]
    D4 --> D5["process + embed"]
    D5 --> D6["save AnnData .h5ad"]
    D3 -->|"yes"| D6
    D6 --> D7["get_tensor() / get_idx_split()"]
    C3 --> E["Ready: analysis, benchmarks, generation"]
    D7 --> E
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L96-L117), [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L1-L13), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L27-L50)

## Step 1: Install and Verify

The repository is self-contained for the records path. Clone it and confirm your Python environment has the few libraries the quick-start code imports:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase.git
cd OpenPhase
python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"
```

For the records path, `pandas` is all you need. For the embedded-dataset path (Step 4), you will additionally need `torch`, `anndata`, `loguru`, `scikit-learn`, and `pydantic`; the benchmark scripts also use `optuna` and `swanlab`. One non-obvious rule: **run Python from the repository root**, because the `zhanglab/` loaders import `meta_config.py` and `meta_embed.py` from the root and rely on relative path setup.

| Dependency group | Packages | Needed for |
|---|---|---|
| Records path | `pandas` | Steps 2–3 of this guide |
| Embedded datasets | `torch`, `anndata`, `loguru`, `scikit-learn`, `pydantic` | Step 4, `zhanglab/` loaders |
| Benchmark scripts | `optuna`, `swanlab` (+ above) | `task1.py`, `task2.py` |

> [!TIP]
> Always launch Python from the `OpenPhase/` root directory. The loaders in `zhanglab/` explicitly resolve `meta_config.py` and `meta_embed.py` relative to the root, so importing them from a subdirectory will fail with `ModuleNotFoundError` even though the package is installed.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L88-L94), [zhanglab/README.md](zhanglab/README.md#L9-L10), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L17-L21)

## Step 2: Load Your First Records

The module `openphase_systems.py` is the recommended entry point: it reads the merged, de-duplicated, condition-level records that are organized **by system** (the set of experiment components, without concentrations). Four systems ship with the repository, and all counts below come straight from the shipped metadata file `data/systems.tsv`:

| System | Meaning | Records | Positive / Negative |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `protein` | protein only | 7,490 | 4,416 / 3,074 |
| `protein_RNA` | protein + RNA | 2,511 | 1,751 / 760 |
| `protein_DNA` | protein + DNA | 662 | 446 / 216 |
| `protein_csat` | protein, saturation concentration | 776 | no binary label |

The API is three small functions, each returning plain pandas objects:

| Function | Signature | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `list_systems()` | no arguments | DataFrame, one row per system with records/sequences/papers/source counts |
| `load_system(system, source=None)` | system name; optional source prefix like `"RNAPSEC"` | DataFrame of that system's records, with a `system` column inserted |
| `load_all(systems=None)` | optional iterable of system names | `dict` mapping each system name to its records DataFrame |

Try the canonical first commands — this exact snippet appears in both the top-level README and `data/README.md`:

```python
from openphase_systems import list_systems, load_system

list_systems()                      # overview: records, sequences, papers, sources per system
rna = load_system("protein_RNA")    # 2,511 rows as a DataFrame
rna2 = load_system("protein_RNA", source="RNAPSEC")   # keep only rows whose source starts with "RNAPSEC"
```

Two behaviors worth knowing as a beginner: passing an unknown system name raises a clear `ValueError` that lists the valid choices, and the `source` filter is a *prefix* match on the `source` column (so `"LLPSDB_v2"` also matches `"LLPSDB_v2_phase_diagram"`). You can also execute `python openphase_systems.py` directly to print the systems overview.

> [!TIP]
> The `protein_csat` system has no binary label — each row instead carries a measured saturation concentration under columns like `readout_class` and `log10_value_uM`. If your analysis assumes a 0/1 `label`, exclude this system or handle it separately.

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L29-L31), [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L34-L47), [data/systems.tsv](data/systems.tsv#L1-L6), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L15-L19), [README.md](README.md#L96-L105)

## Step 3: Know What a Record Looks Like

Each row in a `records.tsv` is **one experimental condition of one system with its outcome** — a binary phase-separation label, or a saturation-concentration measurement for `protein_csat`. The schema is documented exhaustively in `data/README.md`; here is the abridged map you need to start exploring:

| Column group | Examples | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| identity | `record_id`, `source`, `paper`, `uniprot`, `sequence_state` | provenance and protein identification |
| outcome | `label`, `morphology`, `phase_state`; `log10_value_uM` for csat | the target `y` you predict |
| split groups | `cluster_30`, `cluster_20` | MMseqs2 clusters for leakage-free train/test splits |
| conditions | `log10_protein_conc_uM`, `pH`, `temp_C`, `NaCl_mM`, PEG/Ficoll crowders | the environmental `c` inputs |
| missing-value state | `st_*` flags (`obs`, `miss`, `zero`, `rt`) | how each condition value was resolved |
| nucleic acid | `na_class`, `na_len_log10`, `na_g4` | RNA/DNA partner properties, when present |

Missing values are **not imputed** — an unreported condition is left empty and flagged in its companion `st_*` column, so your preprocessing must decide how to treat them explicitly. Note also that sequence text is deliberately absent from these tables (proteins are identified by UniProt accession + length), and the db2 laboratory-notebook records are not included here at all — they live only behind the archived loaders in Step 4.

For the full column-by-column contract, continue to [Condition-Level Record Schema](7-condition-level-record-schema); for systematic per-system loading recipes, see [Loading Records by System](3-loading-records-by-system).

Sources: [data/README.md](data/README.md#L1-L12), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L30-L41), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L43-L48)

## Step 4 (Optional): Build an Embedded Dataset with the Archived Loaders

When you are ready to train models, use the `zhanglab/` loaders — one per original source: `DB1Dataset` (LLPSDB v2), `DB2Dataset` (laboratory notebooks), `DB3Dataset` (RNAPSEC). Each is a PyTorch `Dataset` that runs a fully automatic pipeline on construction: it downloads the raw upstream files if absent, parses and filters them for your chosen system, computes protein/nucleic-acid/condition embeddings from your configuration, and caches everything as an AnnData `.h5ad` file.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["DBxDataset(root='./data', system=..., embedding_config=...)"] --> B{"Raw data present?"}
    B -->|no| C["download upstream source"]
    B -->|yes| D
    C --> D["process raw → system tables"]
    D --> E{"Embeddings present?"}
    E -->|no| F["embed x, na, c per config"]
    E -->|yes| G
    F --> G["save AnnData .h5ad"]
    G --> H["get_tensor() → x, c, y<br/>get_idx_split(split_method=...)"]
```

Embedding choices are configured through `meta_config.create_meta_config()`, which returns a pydantic `MetaEmbeddingConfig` that validates your selections at construction time — invalid names fail fast with the list of allowed options:

| Slot | Allowed values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `protein` | `esmc`, `mtdp`, `rnapsec_protein`, `seq2ind`, `seq2onehot` | `esmc` (factory default: `mtdp`) |
| `dna_rna` | `rnapsec_rna`, `dictionary` | `dictionary` |
| `condition` | `droppler`, `rnapsec_condition`, `rnapsec_condition_class` | `droppler` |

A minimal end-to-end invocation (the same pattern used inside the benchmark scripts) looks like this:

```python
from zhanglab.db1 import DB1Dataset
from meta_config import create_meta_config

cfg = create_meta_config(protein="mtdp", dna_rna="dictionary", condition="droppler")
dataset = DB1Dataset(root="./data", name="DB1", system="protein(1)", embedding_config=cfg)

x, c, y = dataset.get_tensor()               # components, conditions, outcome
train_idx, test_idx = dataset.get_idx_split(split_method="random")
```

The constructor's own docstring uses exactly this two-call pattern, and the benchmark script `task1.py` shows it in a realistic context — building the config, constructing `DB1Dataset`, extracting tensors, and requesting a split in ten lines. The trade-off to understand as a beginner: this path needs network access on first use and more installed packages, but in exchange you get model-ready tensors and embedding machinery; the Step-2 path is instant and offline but returns raw tabular records. For a deeper comparison, continue to [Building Source Datasets with Loaders](5-building-source-datasets-with-loaders) and [Embedding Configuration Matrix](11-embedding-configuration-matrix).

Sources: [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L27-L50), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L76-L119), [meta_config.py](meta_config.py#L5-L14), [meta_config.py](meta_config.py#L38-L41), [task1.py](task1.py#L87-L94), [task1.py](task1.py#L101)

## Where the Quick-Start Outputs Fit in the Repository

The two paths converge on the canonical benchmark tasks: **Task 1** predicts whether a system undergoes phase separation from components + conditions, **Task 2** infers the conditions that produce an outcome (a conditional VAE over phase diagrams), and **Task 3** generates protein sequences for target phase behavior. The quick-start code you just ran is the data layer underneath all three.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Ship["Ships in the repo (offline, pandas-only)"]
        ST["data/systems.tsv"] --> LS["list_systems()"]
        T1["data/protein/records.tsv"] --> LD["load_system()"]
        T2["data/protein_RNA/records.tsv"] --> LD
        T3["data/protein_DNA/records.tsv"] --> LD
        T4["data/protein_csat/records.tsv"] --> LD
    end
    subgraph Zhang["zhanglab/ (online on first run)"]
        DB1["db1: LLPSDB v2"] --> PROC["process + embed"]
        DB2["db2: lab notebooks"] --> PROC
        DB3["db3: RNAPSEC"] --> PROC
        MC["meta_config.py"] -.->|embedding_config| PROC
        PROC --> H5[("AnnData .h5ad")]
    end
    LS --> EXP["records_space/ explorer site"]
    LD --> DF["DataFrames: schema exploration, baselines"]
    H5 --> TASK1["task1.py: outcome prediction"]
    H5 --> TASK2["task2.py: PhaseCVAE condition inference"]
```

For orientation, the annotated tree of the files you touched today:

```
OpenPhase/
├── data/                    ← Step 2–3: records by system, ships with repo
│   ├── systems.tsv          ← what list_systems() reads
│   └── <system>/records.tsv ← what load_system() reads
├── openphase_systems.py     ← Step 2: the three loading functions
├── meta_config.py           ← Step 4: validated embedding configuration
├── zhanglab/                ← Step 4: db1/db2/db3 archived source loaders
├── task1.py / task2.py      ← benchmark scripts consuming the datasets
└── params_all.yaml          ← hyperparameter grid used by the benchmarks
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L58-L69), [README.md](README.md#L71-L86), [params_all.yaml](params_all.yaml#L1-L32), [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L19-L26)

## Verify and Troubleshoot

Run this one-liner as a smoke test; success prints the four systems with their record counts:

```bash
python openphase_systems.py
```

If anything fails, the cause is almost always in this table:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `ValueError: unknown system '...'` | typo or non-system string passed to `load_system` | use a name from `list_systems()`: `protein`, `protein_RNA`, `protein_DNA`, `protein_csat` |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: meta_config` | running Python from a subdirectory | `cd` back to the `OpenPhase/` root before importing `zhanglab` |
| `AssertionError: System ... is not in the list` | system string not valid for that source loader | each `DBxDataset` has its own `system_list` (e.g. `"protein(1)"`, `"protein(2) + RNA"`); check the loader's docstring |
| Download stalls on first `DB1Dataset(...)` | network needed for LLPSDB v2 zip files | the loaders retry on next construction; artifacts are cached as `.h5ad` afterwards |
| `ImportError` for `torch`/`anndata` | missing packages for the embedded path | install the embedded-dataset dependency group from the Step 1 table |

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L50-L51), [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L36-L42), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L101-L106), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L111-L119)

## Where to Go Next

You now hold the two skills the rest of the documentation builds on: reading merged records and constructing embedded datasets. A recommended progression through the catalog:

| Next step | Why now | Link |
|---|---|---|
| Loading recipes per system | go deeper on filtering, sources, and the csat system | [Loading Records by System](3-loading-records-by-system) |
| Visual exploration of the record map | see 11,439 records and the protein universe in your browser — no code | [Interactive Explorer Tour](4-interactive-explorer-tour) |
| Loader internals and artifacts | how `db1`/`db2`/`db3` produce `.h5ad` datasets | [Building Source Datasets with Loaders](5-building-source-datasets-with-loaders) |
| Big-picture architecture | how data, embeddings, and models relate | [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview) |
| First benchmark | train the Task 1 outcome-prediction baselines you saw referenced in `task1.py` | [Outcome Prediction Baselines](8-outcome-prediction-baselines) |

![Protein-only systems in the OpenPhase explorer](https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase/blob/main/assets/fig-protein1-systems.webp?raw=true)


# Loading Records by System



Every machine-learning task in OpenPhase starts with the same raw material: **condition-level records** of protein phase-separation experiments. Rather than forcing you to re-download and re-parse four heterogeneous source databases, the repository ships a small loader module — `openphase_systems.py` — that reads pre-merged tables, one folder per *system*. This page walks you through that loader end to end: what a "system" is, the three public functions you will actually call, how source filtering works, and how to interpret the DataFrame you get back. Everything here assumes only basic Python and pandas familiarity.

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](/openphase_systems.py#L1-L13), [data/README.md](/data/README.md#L1-L5)

## What You Are Loading: Systems and Records

OpenPhase organizes experiments into four **systems**. A system is defined by the *set of components* of the experiment (ignoring concentrations): protein alone, protein with RNA, protein with DNA, or protein with a measured **saturation concentration** (c_sat) readout. A **record** is one experimental condition within a system together with its outcome — either a binary label (phase separation happened or not) or, for the c_sat system, a numeric measurement.

The four systems live as separate folders under `data/`, each containing one tab-separated table:

| System key | Folder | Description | Records | Sequences | UniProt | Papers | Positive / Negative |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `protein` | `protein/` | protein only | 7,490 | 1,163 | 311 | 364 | 4,416 / 3,074 |
| `protein_RNA` | `protein_RNA/` | protein + RNA | 2,511 | 241 | 85 | 125 | 1,751 / 760 |
| `protein_DNA` | `protein_DNA/` | protein + DNA | 662 | 99 | 42 | 41 | 446 / 216 |
| `protein_csat` | `protein_csat/` | protein, saturation concentration | 776 | 42 | 3 | 2 | no binary label |

In the three binary systems, a nucleic acid — when present — is just one of the experimental conditions, encoded in the `na_*` columns. Importantly, the tables deliberately **do not contain sequence text, embeddings, or free-text source fields**; sequences are identified by UniProt accession and length. This keeps the tables a compact, processed benchmark view rather than a replacement for the upstream databases.

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](/openphase_systems.py#L5-L26), [data/README.md](/data/README.md#L3-L13), [data/README.md](/data/README.md#L42-L46)

![protein system illustration](<https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase/blob/main/assets/fig-protein1-systems.webp?raw=true>)

## The Loader API at a Glance

The entire public API is three functions in `openphase_systems.py`. The module resolves its data directory relative to its own file location (`DATA_DIR`), so it works regardless of your current working directory. Internally it is a thin, honest wrapper around `pandas.read_csv` with `sep="\t"` — no hidden downloads, no caching layers, no surprises.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Disk["Files on disk"]
        T1["data/systems.tsv<br/>(per-system inventory)"]
        T2["data/{system}/records.tsv<br/>(4 folders, one per system)"]
    end
    subgraph API["openphase_systems.py"]
        F1["list_systems()"]
        F2["load_system(system, source=None)"]
        F3["load_all(systems=None)"]
    end
    subgraph Result["What you get"]
        R1["DataFrame: inventory<br/>system, records, sources, pos/neg"]
        R2["DataFrame: condition-level records<br/>+ injected system column"]
        R3["Dict: system name to DataFrame"]
    end
    T1 --> F1 --> R1
    T2 --> F2 --> R2
    F2 --> F3 --> R3
```

| Function | Signature | Reads | Returns | Key behavior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `list_systems()` | no arguments | `data/systems.tsv` | `pd.DataFrame` | One row per system: records, sequences, UniProt accessions, papers, per-source counts, positive/negative split |
| `load_system()` | `system: str`, `source: Optional[str] = None` | `data/<system>/records.tsv` | `pd.DataFrame` | Validates the system name, injects a `system` column at position 1, optionally filters rows by source prefix, resets the index |
| `load_all()` | `systems: Optional[Iterable[str]] = None` | all four (or your subset) | `Dict[str, pd.DataFrame]` | Calls `load_system` once per system; omit the argument to load everything |

The minimal two-liner from the data README is the idiomatic entry point:

```python
from openphase_systems import list_systems, load_system
list_systems()
rna = load_system("protein_RNA")   # or load_system("protein_RNA", source="RNAPSEC")
```

Running the module directly (`python openphase_systems.py`) prints the inventory table, which is a quick sanity check that your checkout is intact.

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](/openphase_systems.py#L19-L31), [openphase_systems.py](/openphase_systems.py#L34-L51), [data/README.md](/data/README.md#L15-L19)

## Loading One System with load_system()

Calling `load_system("protein")` performs four verifiable steps in order. First, it validates your argument against the `SYSTEMS` dictionary — the four keys listed above — and raises a `ValueError` naming the valid choices if you mistype. Second, it reads `data/<system>/records.tsv` as a tab-separated CSV with `low_memory=False` (the condition columns mix types, so pandas should not guess chunk-by-chunk). Third, it inserts a `system` column at position 1, right next to `record_id`, so a merged frame is never ambiguous about its origin. Fourth, it applies the optional source filter and resets the index so row numbers are contiguous.

```python
from openphase_systems import load_system

protein = load_system("protein")          # 7,490 rows, all sources
rnapsec = load_system("protein_RNA", source="RNAPSEC")   # source-filtered subset
```

A sample of what comes back — taken verbatim from the first data rows of `data/protein/records.tsv`:

| Column | Example value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `record_id` | `llpsdb2:PS00000046` | globally unique ID, prefixed by source |
| `source` | `LLPSDB_v2` | provenance database |
| `paper` | `pmid:26317470` | PMID or DOI of the originating paper |
| `uniprot` / `protein_name` / `seq_len` | `P35637` / `FUS` / `526` | sequence identity triple |
| `system_id` | `4a254ab17fd6` | hash of the component set |
| `label` | `1` | 1 = phase separation, 0 = none |
| `log10_protein_conc_uM` / `pH` / `temp_C` | `-0.09691` / `7.4` / `22.0` | experimental conditions |

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](/openphase_systems.py#L34-L42), [data/protein/records.tsv](/data/protein/records.tsv#L1-L3)

> [!TIP]
> The `system` column is *injected*, not stored on disk — `records.tsv` on disk starts with `record_id`, `source`, `paper`… and only gains `system` at position 1 when you call `load_system()`. If you ever read a `records.tsv` with raw `pandas.read_csv`, the `system` column will be missing; that is expected, not corruption.

## Filtering by Source — and the Prefix-Matching Rule

Each system aggregates multiple upstream sources. `list_systems()` surfaces the exact per-source counts in its `sources` column (semicolon-separated `name count` pairs), so you can decide which slice you want before loading. For example, `protein` combines five sources and `protein_RNA` also combines five, while `protein_csat` comes from exactly two papers (Bremer 2022 and Ausserwöger 2025).

| System | Sources and record counts (from `systems.tsv`) |
|---|---|
| `protein` | LLPSDB_v2_phase_diagram 3,656; LLPSDB_v2_site 1,707; LLPSDB_v2 1,375; LLPSense 461; PhaSepDB3_pilot_LLM 291 |
| `protein_RNA` | RNAPSEC 1,141; LLPSDB_v2_site 536; LLPSDB_v2_phase_diagram 515; LLPSDB_v2 284; PhaSepDB3_pilot_LLM 35 |
| `protein_DNA` | LLPSDB_v2_phase_diagram 329; LLPSDB_v2_site 197; LLPSDB_v2 90; PhaSepDB3_pilot_LLM 46 |
| `protein_csat` | Bremer2022 410; Ausserwoger2025 366 |

> [!TIP]
> The `source` argument is a **prefix match** (`df["source"].str.startswith(source)`), not an equality test. Passing `source="LLPSDB_v2"` to `load_system("protein")` returns rows from *all three* LLPSDB v2 variants — `LLPSDB_v2`, `LLPSDB_v2_site`, and `LLPSDB_v2_phase_diagram` — because their source strings share that prefix. To isolate one variant, pass the full name, e.g. `source="LLPSDB_v2_phase_diagram"`.

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](/openphase_systems.py#L40-L41), [data/systems.tsv](/data/systems.tsv#L1-L5), [data/README.md](/data/README.md#L21-L25)

## Reading the Returned DataFrame

The record schema is organized into column groups documented in `data/README.md`. The table below is the map you will reach for on day one; the full per-column detail belongs to the [Condition-Level Record Schema](7-condition-level-record-schema) deep-dive page.

| Group | Columns | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | `record_id`, `system`, `source`, `paper`, `uniprot`, `protein_name`, `seq_len`, `sequence_state`, `system_id`, `mutation`, `fusion`, `cleaved`, `ptm` | Which protein construct, from which paper and database |
| Outcome | `label`, `morphology`, `phase_state`; for c_sat: `readout_class`, `log10_value_uM`, `scan_axis` | Did it phase-separate (binary) or the measured saturation value |
| Split groups | `cluster_30`, `cluster_20` | MMseqs2 clusters at 30 % / 20 % identity (coverage 80 %) for leakage-safe train/test splits |
| Conditions | `log10_protein_conc_uM`, `pH`, `temp_C`, `MgCl2_mM`, `NaCl_mM`, `KCl_mM`, `ionic_strength_mM`, crowders `PEG1k`…`Glycerol` | The experimental variables |
| Buffer & additives | `buf_*`, `add_*` | 0/1 flags for buffer families and additive classes |
| Missing-value state | `st_*` (one next to each condition) | `obs` observed, `miss` missing, `zero` reported absent, `rt` room temperature, `none`/`other` for buffer/additive |
| Nucleic acid | `na_class`, `na_len_log10`, `na_conc_log10`, `na_gc`, `na_g4`, … | Nucleic-acid conditions in the RNA/DNA systems |
| Link | `binary_record_with_same_protein` | Relation between c_sat rows and binary records of the same protein |

Two conventions matter for correct downstream use. First, **missing values are never imputed**: an unreported value stays empty in the numeric column and is flagged in its paired `st_*` column (for instance `st_temp` = `rt` means the temperature was only reported as "room temperature", stored as 22 °C). Second, on `protein_csat` rows the binary `label` is empty by design — the outcome is the continuous `log10_value_uM`, classified into readout classes like `dilute`, `csat_boundary`, and `cloud_point`. Plan for that asymmetry before training a single classifier across systems.

Sources: [data/README.md](/data/README.md#L27-L40), [data/protein/records.tsv](/data/protein/records.tsv#L2-L3)

## Loading Several Systems at Once

When you need the full benchmark in memory, `load_all()` returns a dictionary keyed by system name. Because it simply loops over `load_system`, every dictionary value carries the injected `system` column and behaves exactly like an individually loaded frame.

```python
from openphase_systems import load_all

everything = load_all()                                # all four systems
binary_only = load_all(["protein", "protein_RNA", "protein_DNA"])   # your subset
```

The full data footprint is deliberately small — a few text tables — so keeping all four systems in memory is unremarkable on any modern machine. There is no lazy-loading or streaming machinery to learn.

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](/openphase_systems.py#L45-L47)

## Where the Records Come From, and the Archived Loaders

The merged tables were built from five upstream efforts: LLPSDB v2 (download files, website-only rows, and digitized phase-diagram tables), LLPSense, RNAPSEC, a language-model-assisted pilot extraction of three PhaSepDB papers (`PhaSepDB3_pilot_LLM`), plus Bremer 2022 and Ausserwöger 2025 for the c_sat system. One historical source is intentionally absent: the laboratory-notebook records (`db2`) are **not** in these tables.

The repository also preserves the *first-generation* loaders in `zhanglab/`, one per source — `db1.py` (LLPSDB v2), `db2.py` (laboratory notebooks), `db3.py` (RNAPSEC). Unlike the merged system tables, each archived loader downloads raw data from upstream, parses it, embeds it, and packages it as an AnnData (`.h5ad`) PyTorch `Dataset` (see `DB1Dataset`, which handles downloading, filtering, embedding, and split strategies in one class). These are the building blocks used by the benchmark tasks and the embedding pipeline — `task1.py`, for instance, consumes such a dataset via `system_dataset.get_tensor()` before standardizing features for its baselines. If your goal is model training rather than table exploration, that is your next stop: [Building Source Datasets with Loaders](5-building-source-datasets-with-loaders).

Sources: [data/README.md](/data/README.md#L21-L25), [zhanglab/README.md](/zhanglab/README.md#L1-L13), [zhanglab/db1.py](/zhanglab/db1.py#L27-L38), [task1.py](/task1.py#L26-L37)

## Quick Troubleshooting Reference

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `ValueError: unknown system 'protein-rna'` | System keys are exact and case-sensitive: `protein`, `protein_RNA`, `protein_DNA`, `protein_csat` | Use `list_systems()` first, then copy the key verbatim |
| Source filter returns "too many" rows | `source` is a prefix match (`startswith`), so short prefixes match multiple variants | Pass the complete source string, e.g. `LLPSDB_v2_phase_diagram` |
| `label` column has empty values | You loaded `protein_csat`, whose outcome is `log10_value_uM` with no binary label | Treat c_sat as a regression/ordinal problem, or exclude it from classification |
| Sequence text is nowhere in the frame | By design: sequences are identified by `uniprot` + `seq_len`, text lives upstream | Fetch sequences separately; see the embedding pages |
| Unexpected `NaN` in condition columns | Unreported values stay empty and are flagged in `st_*` — they are never imputed | Filter or handle using the `st_*` flags before modeling |

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](/openphase_systems.py#L36-L41), [data/README.md](/data/README.md#L32-L42)

## Suggested Reading Path

You now know how to pull any system's records into a pandas DataFrame in one line. From here, the catalog offers three natural directions depending on your goal: tour the records visually in the browser with [Interactive Explorer Tour](4-interactive-explorer-tour); learn how the per-source `zhanglab` datasets wrap these records with embeddings for training in [Building Source Datasets with Loaders](5-building-source-datasets-with-loaders); or study every column group in depth in [Condition-Level Record Schema](7-condition-level-record-schema). When you are ready to train, [Outcome Prediction Baselines](8-outcome-prediction-baselines) shows the end-to-end consumption pattern of the loaders in real benchmark code.


# Interactive Explorer Tour



The Records Space Explorer is OpenPhase's browser-based window into the curated LLPS record dataset: a single interactive scatter map where every dot is one experimental record, plus a "Try your own experiment" mode that places *your* hypothetical protein-condition combination onto the same map — entirely in the browser, with no server and no network calls. This page is a guided tour of that interface: how to open it, what each pane and control does, and how the pieces fit together. For the statistical model running under the hood, see [Record Map Distance Model](19-record-map-distance-model); for how the whole website is generated, see [Site Build Pipeline](21-site-build-pipeline).

## What You Are Touring: One Self-Contained Page

The explorer ships as a **self-contained HTML file**: build script `rs05_build_explorer.py` packs coordinates, labels, condition fields, embeddings, and a protein universe into one data blob and injects it — together with three JavaScript modules — into the template `explorer_template.html`. The build produces two artifacts: `records_space_explorer.html`, which you can open directly in any browser, and `page_fragment.html` for embedding elsewhere. The page contains coordinates and annotations (protein names, UniProt IDs, paper IDs, conditions, readouts) but **no protein sequences**, keeping the file light.

Sources: [rs05_build_explorer.py](records_space/scripts/rs05_build_explorer.py#L2-L4), [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L213-L217)

## How to Open the Explorer

There are three entry points, all fed by the same build pipeline. Locally, run the build script and open `explorer/records_space_explorer.html`. For publication, `rs17_build_site.py` stages a GitHub Pages directory where `site/records_space/index.html` *is* the explorer. Finally, the home page (`site/index.html`) embeds clickable hotzones and chips over its figure images that deep-link into the explorer with pre-applied filters — for example, clicking the "protein + RNA" region lands on `records_space/#na=RNA&csat=hide`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[CSV tables<br/>rs_plot_table.tsv / rs_coords.tsv] --> B["rs05_build_explorer.py<br/>pack data + inject JS"]
    T[explorer_template.html] --> B
    J[js/ modules<br/>condition_parser · records_space · try_panel] --> B
    B --> C[records_space_explorer.html<br/>open directly in browser]
    B --> D[page_fragment.html]
    C --> E["rs17_build_site.py<br/>stage GitHub Pages site"]
    E --> F[site/records_space/index.html<br/>linked from home page hotzones]
```

![OpenPhase main figure — home page image whose hotzones deep-link into the explorer](https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase/blob/main/assets/openphase-main.webp?raw=true)

Sources: [rs05_build_explorer.py](records_space/scripts/rs05_build_explorer.py#L2-L4), [rs17_build_site.py](records_space/scripts/rs17_build_site.py#L2-L7), [rs17_build_site.py](records_space/scripts/rs17_build_site.py#L36-L52)

## Architecture at a Glance

Understanding the file's composition makes the rest of the tour easier to follow. The template reserves four placeholder slots, and the build script fills them in. Three slots receive the JavaScript modules from `records_space/explorer/js/`; the fourth receives a base64-packed JSON `DATA` object holding all coordinates, categories, and the protein universe.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Single HTML page
        P1["ConditionParser<br/>(condition_parser.js)<br/>free-text → structured conditions"] --> APP
        P2["RecordsSpace.Space<br/>(records_space.js)<br/>sequence matching + distances"] --> APP
        P3["initTryPanel<br/>(try_panel.js)<br/>'Try your own experiment' form"] --> APP
        P4["DATA blob<br/>coords · categories · universe<br/>tools masks · example defs"] --> APP
        APP["Main script (template)<br/>map canvas · filters · legend · cards"] --> CANVAS[&lt;canvas&gt; scatter map]
    end
```

All four components run **fully offline in your browser**: the `RecordsSpace` module explicitly states it never touches the network and processes all input within the page — relevant if you paste proprietary sequences into Try mode.

Sources: [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L213-L217), [records_space.js](records_space/explorer/js/records_space.js#L1-L2)

## The Three-Pane Layout

On a wide screen the page is a three-column grid: a **control rail** on the left, the square **map stage** in the middle, and a sticky **record card** on the right. The grid reflows at two breakpoints — below 760 px everything stacks vertically, and between 760 px and 960 px the rail and card sit under the map — so the explorer works on phones too.

| Pane | HTML root | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Control rail | `<aside id="rail">` | Record-type toggles, condition filters, text search, point size, reset |
| Map stage | `<main class="stage">` | Lens/color/style selectors, zoomable canvas, highlight note, glyph key, legend |
| Record card | `<section id="card">` | Details of the hovered or pinned point, with quick actions |

Sources: [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L27-L30), [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L173-L210)

## Explore Mode: The Control Rail

Explore mode is the default. The rail filters which records are visible; every change triggers `applyFilters()`, which recomputes a visibility array over all records before the canvas redraws. Filtering is purely conjunctive — a record stays visible only if it passes every active filter.

| Control | Options | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Show checkboxes | Binary records / csat records | Include or exclude non-quantitative records vs. saturation (csat) records |
| Nucleic acid | Any / None / RNA / DNA | Keep records matching the nucleic-acid class |
| Temperature | Measured / Room temp. only / Missing + min–max °C range | Filter by temperature state and numeric band |
| csat link | Any / csat record / identical sequence to csat / same UniProt as csat | Filter by relationship to the saturation-measurement pool |
| Find protein, paper or record | free text | Substring search over name, UniProt, paper, record ID, entry — e.g. `FUS`, `P35637`, `pmid:29064502` |
| Point size | slider 1–6 | Adjust dot radius |
| Reset view and filters | button | Restore every control and the zoom to defaults |

Sources: [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L175-L190), [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L301-L319), [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L749-L752)

## The Map Stage: Lenses, Colors, and Styles

Above the canvas, the toolbar chooses **how** the records are drawn. The **Map** selector picks one of five precomputed projections ("lenses"), each normalizing coordinates into the unit square with north-up orientation at build time. The **Color by** selector recolors every point by any categorical field (protein identity, construct type, phase-separation label, source database, …) or continuous field (temperature, pH, NaCl, NCPR, aromatic fraction, …), and the **Legend** below the map lists each color group — click a legend entry to hide or show that group. **Style** switches between solid blobs, soft glow, and dots only; **Outline** adds light, colored, dashed, or contour-ring edges.

| Lens key | Label | What it emphasizes |
|---|---|---|
| `tsne_full` | t-SNE · full | Default view; cluster shape over all features |
| `umap_full` | UMAP · full | UMAP over protein + condition features |
| `umap_prot` | UMAP · protein only | Sequence-driven structure |
| `umap_cond` | UMAP · nucleic acid + conditions | Condition-driven structure |
| `umap_fullM` | UMAP · full, observed-only (M−) | Complete-observation subset |
| `umap_universe` | (protein universe) | Records **plus** ring glyphs for proteins without records |

On the canvas itself: **scroll to zoom, drag to pan, click a point to pin it**; the `+` / `−` / `Fit` buttons control zoom explicitly, and the counter in the corner reports how many points are visible.

Sources: [rs05_build_explorer.py](records_space/scripts/rs05_build_explorer.py#L20-L21), [rs05_build_explorer.py](records_space/scripts/rs05_build_explorer.py#L48-L56), [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L192-L208), [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L264-L287)

## Highlighting Tool Entries and the Protein Universe

The **Highlight tool entries** selector overlays the member set of an external tool or database (LLPSDB v2, PhaSepDB 3 pilot, LLPSense, RNAPSEC, Bremer 2022, Ausserwöger 2025, and others) onto the map. Each record carries a compact **bitmask** of tool memberships (two 32-bit words per record), so membership tests are cheap array lookups, and the selector groups options by tool family with live counts. Two glyph kinds exist, explained by the glyph key under the canvas: **filled dots are records with conditions**, **hollow rings are proteins mentioned by a tool but lacking any condition data** (the "protein universe"). Selecting a protein-only tool automatically switches the lens to `umap_universe` so its rings are visible, and a note bar under the canvas reports counts — e.g. "N proteins in the map · M more without records" — with a button to show all universe members.

Hovering or pinning a ring opens a universe card: accession, organism, length, the tools mentioning it, and the **closest protein that does have records** with its cosine similarity. From there, one click hands the protein to Try mode.

Sources: [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L206), [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L221-L230), [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L753-L788), [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L813-L849)

## Reading a Record: The Detail Card

Clicking any filled dot pins it and fills the right-hand card: protein name and UniProt ID, paper link, source entry, construct type, quantitative readout class, plus a key/value table of conditions (temperature, pH, salts, crowder, buffer, other solutes, nucleic acid with length and ratio) and a count of missing dimensions. Three quick actions turn a single record into a new query without retyping: **Highlight this protein** and **Highlight this paper** fill the search box, and **Same temperature ±2 °C** sets the temperature range filter around the pinned record.

Sources: [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L700-L714)

## Try Your Own Experiment: Step by Step

The header's second mode button swaps the rail for the **Try** pane. You describe a hypothetical experiment; the page computes its protein embedding, its distances to every record, and drops a pink **star** on the map at the inverse-distance-weighted centroid of its 8 nearest neighbors, with rings marking those neighbors. A color-coded **verdict** (green = good, amber = moderate, red = poor phase-separation outlook) and a neighbor list with per-database pills summarize the result; neighbor confidence uses a Wilson interval. Three input paths feed the same pipeline:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["1 · Protein"] --> P1{Source?}
    P1 -->|Pick example| A["Curated examples<br/>example_defs.json"]
    P1 -->|Load tool entry| B["Bitmask lookup in<br/>universe / dataset"]
    P1 -->|Paste sequence| C["analyzeSequence()<br/>FNV-1a hash + 5-mer sketch"]
    C --> D{Match class?}
    D -->|exact| E1["Exact ESMC embedding<br/>from dataset"]
    D -->|variant / Colab-exact| E2["Precomputed exact<br/>or closest construct"]
    D -->|novel| E3["In-browser approximate<br/>embedding (warns: rough)"]
    T["2 · Conditions<br/>quick-fill text OR manual fields"] --> F[CondParser<br/>routes text → values]
    A --> G[Compute distances<br/>to all records]
    B --> G
    E1 --> G
    E2 --> G
    E3 --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H["Star on map + rings<br/>verdict + neighbor list"]
```

**Step 1 — Protein.** Either start from a curated example (grouped, e.g. "New proteins (no record in the dataset)" with GRB2 in HEPES/KCl/MgCl₂/PEG 8000), load an entry from any highlighted tool, or paste an amino-acid sequence (FASTA headers are stripped automatically). A checkbox lets you treat the protein and its relatives as unseen. A short info box then reports what happened: length, molecular weight, match class, and which embedding strategy was used.

**Step 2 — Conditions.** The fastest route is the quick-fill textarea: type a sentence like `20 mM Tris pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 25 °C, 20 µM protein, 1 mM DTT` and `CondParser` — a JavaScript port of the dataset's own Python parsing engine, sharing its unit tables, PEG bins, and salt aliases — fills every field for you to inspect and correct. You can also fill manually: temperature (with an RT chip for "room temperature only, no number given"), pH, protein µM, buffer family, NaCl/KCl/MgCl₂ in mM, crowder and percentage, nucleic-acid kind/type/length/concentration, and additive chips (DTT/TCEP, EDTA, detergents, 1,6-hexanediol, …). Empty boxes mean unknown; once any salt is given, empty salts count as none.

**Sequence classification, in detail.** This is the heart of Try mode, and worth understanding as a beginner:

| Class | Criterion | Protein embedding used |
|---|---|---|
| `exact` | Identical sequence in dataset (double 32-bit hash + length) | Dataset's exact ESMC embedding |
| Colab-exact | Sequence listed in `unseen_examples.fasta` with precomputed vector | Exact embedding computed offline, stored in the page |
| `variant` | ≥50% of query 5-mers contained in a known construct (or ≥30% Jaccard) | Embedding of the closest known construct |
| `related` | A few shared 5-mers (below variant thresholds) | Closest construct embedding |
| `novel` | No similar sequence | Approximate regression embedding |

For novel sequences the page embeds via `approxZ()` — a lightweight regression from amino-acid composition and dimer features — and shows an explicit warning that no ESMC model runs in the browser, quoting held-out recovery statistics so you know how much to trust the placement. Under **Advanced** you can force the approximation even where an exact embedding exists, or copy a request string to obtain an exact embedding offline and, if it is added to the examples file, it will be used automatically on your next visit.

Sources: [try_panel.js](records_space/explorer/js/try_panel.js#L1-L3), [try_panel.js](records_space/explorer/js/try_panel.js#L28-L78), [try_panel.js](records_space/explorer/js/try_panel.js#L90-L135), [records_space.js](records_space/explorer/js/records_space.js#L75-L100), [condition_parser.js](records_space/explorer/js/condition_parser.js#L1-L9), [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L851-L879), [example_defs.json](records_space/explorer/examples/example_defs.json#L1)

## Shareable Views: URL Deep Links

Every interesting view is reproducible through the URL fragment — this is exactly how the home page hotzones work. `applyHash()` reads parameters after the `#`, validates each against its dropdown's options, and applies them on load:

| Parameter | Example | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `na` | `#na=RNA` | Nucleic-acid filter (RNA / DNA / none) |
| `csat` | `#csat=only` or `#csat=hide` | Show only csat records, or hide them |
| `hl` | `#hl=llpsdb` | Highlight a tool entry set |
| `q` | `#q=FUS` | Prefill the text search |
| `protein` | `#protein=FUS` | Isolate one protein's records (hides all others) |
| `lens` | `#lens=umap_prot` | Select the map projection |
| `mode` | `#mode=try` | Open directly in Try-your-own-experiment mode |

The theme toggle (moon/sun button) persists your light/dark choice in `localStorage`, and the "← OpenPhase" home link appears only when the page is served from GitHub Pages or localhost.

Sources: [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L715-L734), [explorer_template.html](records_space/explorer/explorer_template.html#L161-L172), [rs17_build_site.py](records_space/scripts/rs17_build_site.py#L62-L64)

## Where to Go Next

You have now toured the explorer end to end. To understand *why* the star lands where it does, continue with [Record Map Distance Model](19-record-map-distance-model); to see how the page, the negatives site, and the protein universe exports are produced, follow [Site Build Pipeline](21-site-build-pipeline) and [Negatives and Protein Universe](20-negatives-and-protein-universe). To work with the underlying records programmatically instead of visually, head to the next catalog page, [Building Source Datasets with Loaders](5-building-source-datasets-with-loaders).


# Building Source Datasets with Loaders



This page covers the **archived source loaders** — `zhanglab/db1.py`, `db2.py`, and `db3.py` — which download raw data from three upstream phase-separation databases, parse it into unified tables, embed it, and persist each result as an AnnData (`.h5ad`) dataset ready for PyTorch training. Where [Loading Records by System](3-loading-records-by-system) showed you how to *read* the pre-merged per-system TSVs, this page shows you how the per-*source* datasets are *built from scratch* — the machinery underneath the benchmark tables.

![OpenPhase system overview](https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase/blob/main/assets/openphase-main.webp?raw=true)

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L10-L12), [zhanglab/README.md](zhanglab/README.md#L1-L9)

## Two Layers of Data Loading: Merged Systems vs. Raw Sources

The repository exposes **two generations of loaders**, and understanding their relationship prevents confusion later. The *current* loader, `openphase_systems.py`, reads the benchmark's merged condition-level records — four systems stored as `data/<system>/records.tsv`: `protein` (7,490 records), `protein_RNA` (2,511), `protein_DNA` (662), and `protein_csat` (776 rows of saturation concentrations). Its API is minimal: `list_systems()` returns a summary table, `load_system(system, source=...)` returns one system as a DataFrame, and `load_all()` returns a dictionary of all systems.

The *archived* loaders in `zhanglab/` are the original build pipeline, one module per upstream source: `db1.py` for **LLPSDB v2**, `db2.py` for **laboratory notebooks** (Zhang lab), and `db3.py` for **RNAPSEC**. They do not read the TSVs — they reach upstream websites themselves, so you can reproduce the raw-to-embedded journey end to end. Note one asymmetry: the lab-notebook records (`db2`) are deliberately **not** included in the merged `data/` tables.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Archived["Archived build pipeline (zhanglab/)"]
        A1["LLPSDB v2 site"] --> B1["db1.py"]
        A2["Google Drive<br/>(Zhang lab notebooks)"] --> B2["db2.py"]
        A3["GitHub: RNAPSEC"] --> B3["db3.py"]
        B1 --> E["Embed via meta_embed.py<br/>+ meta_config.py"]
        B2 --> E
        B3 --> E
        E --> H[("AnnData<br/>.h5ad per source")]
    end
    subgraph Current["Current benchmark loader"]
        T[("data/&lt;system&gt;/records.tsv<br/>merged, source-labelled")] --> O["openphase_systems.py<br/>load_system / load_all"]
    end
    H -.->|"records were merged<br/>+ relabelled by source"| T
```

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L1-L47), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L21-L25), [zhanglab/README.md](zhanglab/README.md#L1-L14), [data/systems.tsv](data/systems.tsv#L1-L6)

## The Three Source Loaders at a Glance

Each loader follows the same class contract (a PyTorch `Dataset` subclass) but differs in its upstream transport and its granularity. The table below is your selection guide:

| | `DB1Dataset` (db1.py) | `DB2Dataset` (db2.py) | `DB3Dataset` (db3.py) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Source** | LLPSDB v2 (bio-comp.org.cn) | Zhang lab experimental notebooks | RNAPSEC / RNAPhaSep literature |
| **Download** | 4 zips via HTTP POST simulation | One XLSX via `gdown` (Google Drive) | One XLSX via `requests` from GitHub |
| **Selection axis** | `system`, e.g. `'protein(1)'`, `'protein(2) + RNA'` | `subset_type`: `'CoREST'`, `'IDR'`, `'RGG'` | whole file (protein+RNA only) |
| **Label semantics** | `'Yes'/'No'` phase separation | binary (IDR has continuous readings) | morphology map: liquid/solid/gel → 1, solute → 0 |
| **Strict filtering** | strict vs. loose system filter | subset filter only | drop rows with any NaN |
| **Output** | `{system}.no_missing.h5ad` | subset `.h5ad` | `rnapsec_no_missing_1298.h5ad` |

Two practical facts to remember: run the imports **from the repository root** (`from zhanglab.db1 import DB1Dataset`), because the archived modules import `meta_config.py` and `meta_embed.py` from the root directory; and DB1 alone knows 14 systems — 7 single-protein variants (`protein(1)`…`protein(7)`), 3 protein+RNA, 4 protein+DNA, plus a `NaN` bucket.

Sources: [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L27-L74), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L124-L131), [zhanglab/db2.py](zhanglab/db2.py#L21-L54), [zhanglab/db2.py](zhanglab/db2.py#L107-L109), [zhanglab/db3.py](zhanglab/db3.py#L17-L44), [zhanglab/db3.py](zhanglab/db3.py#L216-L217), [zhanglab/README.md](zhanglab/README.md#L11-L13)

## The Four-Stage Build Lifecycle

All three loaders share one orchestration pattern, visible in their `__init__` methods: **download → process → embed**, with every stage guarded by an existence check. The first constructor call does the full build; subsequent calls load the cached artifacts instead. This makes the loaders idempotent — instantiate them repeatedly at zero cost, and delete an artifact to force that stage to rerun.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["Instantiate<br/>DB1Dataset(root, system, embedding_config)"] --> C1{"raw/*.xlsx exist?"}
    C1 -- no --> D["download()<br/>4 zips → extract → .xls renamed .xlsx"]
    D --> C2
    C1 -- yes --> C2{"processed/<br/>exp_parsed.txt + system tables exist?"}
    C2 -- no --> P["process_raw()<br/>parse 12 unified columns"]
    P --> PS["process_system()<br/>filter to system, strict + loose"]
    PS --> C3
    C2 -- yes --> C3{"embedding/<br/>.no_missing.h5ad exists?"}
    C3 -- no --> E["embed_system()<br/>x / x_rna / x_dna / c / y"]
    C3 -- yes --> R["Ready:<br/>get_tensor() · get_idx_split()"]
    E --> R
```

Each stage writes into a fixed directory layout under `root/<name>/`: `raw/` holds the untouched upstream files, `processed/` holds the parsed TSVs (`exp_raw.txt`, `exp_parsed.txt`, then per-system `{system}.txt` and `{system}.no_missing.txt`), and `embedding/` holds the final AnnData file. The `process_raw` stage of DB1 is the heaviest — it normalizes free-text spreadsheet columns (temperature ranges, semicolon-separated solute concentrations, buffer pH, crowding agents, nucleic acid names) into twelve canonical columns such as `Phase label`, `Phase system`, `Protein sequences`, and `Ionic strength`; DB3 performs the same normalization against RNAPSEC's own schema, collapsing 1,514 parsed rows to 1,298 fully-observed ones.

> [!TIP]
> Treat `raw/`, `processed/`, and `embedding/` as a build cache. If an upstream website changes its file format mid-project, delete only the affected stage's folder — e.g. remove `DB1/processed/` to re-parse without re-downloading.

Sources: [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L76-L121), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L149-L165), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L167-L233), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L235-L315), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L579-L599), [zhanglab/db2.py](zhanglab/db2.py#L48-L89), [zhanglab/db3.py](zhanglab/db3.py#L40-L79), [zhanglab/db3.py](zhanglab/db3.py#L124-L202)

## Configuring Embeddings: MetaEmbeddingConfig

Every loader accepts a `MetaEmbeddingConfig` object — a small pydantic model defined at the repository root that selects **one embedding per modality**. It validates your choices at construction time, so an invalid model name fails immediately with the allowed set in the error message. The factory function `create_meta_config()` builds one in a single call, and this is where DB1's default (`create_meta_config(protein='mtdp', ...)`) differs from the config class defaults (`esmc`).

| Slot | Field | Allowed values | Default (field) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Protein | `protein_embedding` | `esmc`, `mtdp`, `rnapsec_protein`, `seq2ind`, `seq2onehot` | `esmc` |
| Nucleic acid | `dna_rna_embedding` | `rnapsec_rna`, `dictionary` | `dictionary` |
| Conditions | `condition_embedding` | `droppler`, `rnapsec_condition`, `rnapsec_condition_class` | `droppler` |

```python
from meta_config import create_meta_config
from zhanglab.db1 import DB1Dataset

cfg = create_meta_config(protein="esmc", dna_rna="dictionary", condition="droppler")
dataset = DB1Dataset(root="./data_build", system="protein(1)", embedding_config=cfg, download=True)
```

The full design space — dimensionality, pooling strategies, and which model suits which task — is catalogued in [Embedding Configuration Matrix](11-embedding-configuration-matrix) and [Protein and Nucleic Acid Embeddings](12-protein-and-nucleic-acid-embeddings); here you only need the selection mechanism.

Sources: [meta_config.py](meta_config.py#L1-L41), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L20-L21)

## Inside the Embedding Dispatch Layer

`meta_embed.py` exposes three public functions, and each is a **dispatcher** that maps your config string to a concrete featurizer. This one indirection point is how a single config change swaps the entire featurization stack without touching loader code.

| Function | Model key | Technique | Output shape per record |
|---|---|---|---|
| `get_protein_embeddings` | `esmc` | ESM Cambrian 600M, residue tensor mean-pooled over sequence | 1 vector (pooled) |
| | `mtdp` | MTDP pretrained checkpoint (`./MTDP/models/UniProtKB/UniProtKB.bin`) | 1280-dim |
| | `rnapsec_protein` | 29 Biopython physicochemical features (weight, AA %, GRAVY, pI, helix/turn/sheet…) | 29-dim |
| `get_dna_rna_embeddings` | `dictionary` | name → integer index mapping (for later `nn.Embedding`) | 1 index + mapping dict |
| | `rnapsec_rna` | 97-dim MathFeature k-mer/ORF/entropy/Fourier features via subprocess | 97-dim |
| `get_condition_embeddings` | `droppler` | 14 numeric condition dims (below) | 14-dim |

The **Droppler-style** condition vector is worth understanding because it appears throughout the project: ten one-hot temperature bins (0–100 °C in ten-degree steps, so a range like 25–40 °C lights up several bins), one log10 protein concentration (with a small epsilon added before the log to keep zeros finite), one log10 ionic strength, one crowding-agent binary, and the pH value. Embeddings are computed per *unique sequence* and cached in a dict first, so duplicated proteins across records are featurized only once.

> [!TIP]
> The nucleic-acid `dictionary` mode returns *indices plus a name-to-index mapping* — the mapping is stored in the AnnData `uns` slot, not `obsm`. Downstream models consume the index tensor through an embedding layer, so if you export the `.h5ad` elsewhere, carry `uns` along or your RNA tokens become meaningless integers.

Sources: [meta_embed.py](meta_embed.py#L407-L430), [meta_embed.py](meta_embed.py#L433-L459), [meta_embed.py](meta_embed.py#L462-L586), [meta_embed.py](meta_embed.py#L44-L69), [meta_embed.py](meta_embed.py#L124-L192), [meta_embed.py](meta_embed.py#L195-L317)

## Consuming a Built Dataset: AnnData, Tensors, and Splits

The embedding stage persists everything into one AnnData file. Tensors live in the `obsm` slot under keys that **encode the model that produced them**, and lookup dictionaries go to `uns`:

| Key pattern (in `obsm`) | Contents | Example key |
|---|---|---|
| `x_{protein_model}` | single-protein embeddings | `x_esmc` |
| `x_{i}_{protein_model}` | i-th protein of multi-protein systems | `x_1_mtdp`, `x_2_mtdp` |
| `x_rna_{na_method}` / `x_dna_{na_method}` | nucleic-acid indices or features | `x_rna_dictionary` |
| `c_{condition_model}` | 14-dim condition matrix | `c_droppler` |
| `y` | binary phase-separation labels | `y` |
| `uns: {rna,dna}_mapping_{na_method}` | name → index dictionaries | `rna_mapping_dictionary` |

From there, two accessor methods finish the job. `get_tensor()` reads the `.h5ad` and returns plain float tensors whose arity adapts to the system — `(x, c, y)` for `protein(1)`, `(x1, x2, x_dna, c, y)` for `protein(2) + DNA`, and so on, exactly matching the composition of the system you selected. `get_idx_split(split_method, seed)` returns `(train_idx, test_idx)` with an 80/20 split under seven strategies, from plain `random` to stratification by `phase_label`, binned `temperature`, quantile-binned concentration or ionic strength, crowding-agent presence, or binned pH — a quick ablation toolbox you can extend with the rigorous protocols described in [Split Strategies and Metrics](10-split-strategies-and-metrics).

Sources: [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L317-L336), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L404-L420), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L422-L502), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L504-L573)

## Putting It Together: A Complete Build Session

The snippet below builds the LLPSDB v2 single-protein source dataset from a clean directory and immediately reads it back as training tensors. On first run it downloads four zips, parses, and embeds (GPU is used by the protein embedders by default); on every later run the constructor returns after the existence checks.

```python
from meta_config import create_meta_config
from zhanglab.db1 import DB1Dataset

cfg  = create_meta_config(protein="esmc", dna_rna="dictionary", condition="droppler")
data = DB1Dataset(root="./data_build", name="DB1",
                  system="protein(1)", embedding_config=cfg)

x, c, y      = data.get_tensor()               # (n, d_prot), (n, 14), (n,)
train, test  = data.get_idx_split(split_method="phase_label_stratified", seed=0)
```

Remember the scope of what you just built: this is the **LLPSDB v2 source in isolation**, with sequences and embeddings attached. For benchmarking against the full merged corpus — LLPSDB v2 *plus* LLPSense, RNAPSEC, PhaSepDB-pilot, and the csat sources — go back to `openphase_systems.load_system()` as covered in [Loading Records by System](3-loading-records-by-system), and note that those merged TSVs deliberately exclude sequence text and embeddings ([see what's included](7-condition-level-record-schema)).

Sources: [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L27-L50), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L42-L46)

## Where to Go Next

A suggested reading order from here: solidify the field-level meaning of what these loaders produce with [Condition-Level Record Schema](7-condition-level-record-schema); then understand why embeddings are the lingua franca between heterogeneous sources in [Embedding Configuration Matrix](11-embedding-configuration-matrix) and [Protein and Nucleic Acid Embeddings](12-protein-and-nucleic-acid-embeddings); finally, see how condition vectors like Droppler's 14 dims are engineered in [Condition Feature Engineering](13-condition-feature-engineering). When you're ready to run real benchmarks on the merged tables, continue to [Outcome Prediction Baselines](8-outcome-prediction-baselines).


# Architecture Overview



OpenPhase is organized as a layered system: raw experimental sources flow through loaders and embedding services into benchmarks and generative models, while a parallel build pipeline produces both the merged record tables and an interactive browser-based explorer. This page maps the repository's structural anatomy — the layers, their boundaries, and the contracts between them — so that the Deep Dive pages that follow have a stable frame of reference. Everything here is documented from the code itself; deeper mechanics of each subsystem are deferred to their dedicated pages.

![OpenPhase system-level overview](https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase/blob/main/assets/openphase-main.webp?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L20)

## The Layer Map

The repository decomposes into five cooperating layers plus one upstream build subsystem. Before reading the diagram, two prerequisites: arrows denote *runtime dependency* (a module imports or loads from its target), and the layers are ordered by data direction — raw sources at the left, models at the right. The single most important structural fact is that `data/` is not the raw source: per [data/README.md](data/README.md#L41-L46), the merged system tables are themselves *built from* the records space pipeline, so `records_space/` sits upstream of everything.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    RAW["Raw sources<br/>LLPSDB v2 · LLPSense · RNAPSEC<br/>PhaSepDB3 pilot · Bremer · Ausserwöger"]

    subgraph RS["Build subsystem"]
        SCRIPTS["records_space/<br/>rs01–rs17 scripts + colab drivers"]
    end

    subgraph L1["Layer 1 · Data access"]
        TSV["data/&lt;system&gt;/records.tsv"]
        OPS["openphase_systems.py"]
    end

    subgraph L2["Layer 2 · Source loaders"]
        DB1["DB1Dataset<br/>LLPSDB v2"]
        DB2["DB2Dataset<br/>lab notebooks"]
        DB3["DB3Dataset<br/>RNAPSEC"]
    end

    subgraph L3["Layer 3 · Embedding plane"]
        MC["meta_config.py"]
        ME["meta_embed.py"]
        MTDP["MTDP/<br/>runtime weights"]
    end

    subgraph L4["Layer 4 · Benchmarks"]
        T1["task1.py<br/>outcome prediction"]
        T2["task2.py<br/>PhaseCVAE"]
        PA["params_all.yaml"]
    end

    subgraph L5["Layer 5 · Generative"]
        DIS["Discrete/"]
        LDM["ldm/"]
    end

    RAW --> SCRIPTS
    SCRIPTS --> TSV
    OPS --> TSV
    SCRIPTS --> RSITE["static HTML explorer"]
    DB1 --> ME
    DB2 --> ME
    DB3 --> ME
    ME --> MTDP
    MC -.drives.-> ME
    T1 --> DB1
    T2 --> DB3
    T1 --> MC
    T2 --> MC
    LDM --> PA
```

The build subsystem (`records_space/scripts`, `records_space/colab`) performs the merge and de-duplication of the six sources; its outputs branch into the tabular records consumed by `openphase_systems.py` and the self-contained HTML explorer served by GitHub Pages. Layers 2 and 3 form a vertical pairing — every dataset class delegates embedding work to `meta_embed.py` under a configuration object from `meta_config.py` — and Layers 4 and 5 sit on top as alternative consumers of the same embedded tensors.

Sources: [data/README.md](data/README.md#L41-L46), [records_space/README.md](records_space/README.md#L41-L77), [README.md](README.md#L80-L98)

## The (x, c, y) Contract

The unifying abstraction across every layer is a three-tuple convention: **x** = component sequences (protein, optional RNA/DNA), **c** = experimental conditions, **y** = outcome label. This contract appears identically at every altitude of the stack. The PyTorch dataset in `Discrete/dataset.py` returns exactly `x[idx], c[idx], y[idx]` per sample; the benchmark loader in `task1.py` unpacks `*x, c, y = system_dataset.get_tensor()`; and the `DB1Dataset` docstring documents the same `x, c, y = dataset.get_tensor()` interface for the source-level datasets. Because all consumers speak this contract, swapping an embedding method or a dataset class does not change downstream model code — this is the architectural hinge that makes the hyperparameter grid in `params_all.yaml` composable.

Sources: [Discrete/dataset.py](Discrete/dataset.py#L3-L21), [task1.py](task1.py#L21-L34), [zhanglab/db1.py](zhanglab/db1.py#L42-L70)

## Layer 1 — Data Access: System-Level Records

`openphase_systems.py` is a deliberately thin facade — 52 lines, no classes — over four TSV tables, one per **system** (the set of an experiment's components without concentrations). `list_systems()` returns the summary table `data/systems.tsv`; `load_system(system, source=...)` validates the system name against a literal registry, loads `data/<system>/records.tsv`, injects a `system` column, and optionally filters by source prefix; `load_all()` returns a dictionary of data frames. The merged tables are a *processed benchmarking view*: they deliberately exclude sequence text, embeddings, and free-text source fields, identifying sequences instead by UniProt accession and length, and unreported values are left empty with a state flag (`st_*`) rather than imputed.

| System folder | Contents | Records | Sequences | Label |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| `data/protein/` | protein only | 7,490 | 1,163 | binary |
| `data/protein_RNA/` | protein + RNA | 2,511 | 241 | binary |
| `data/protein_DNA/` | protein + DNA | 662 | 99 | binary |
| `data/protein_csat/` | saturation concentration | 776 | 42 | measured value |

![protein(1) system figure](https://github.com/nicetone9/OpenPhase/blob/main/assets/fig-protein1-systems.webp?raw=true)

Sources: [openphase_systems.py](openphase_systems.py#L18-L43), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L6-L11), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L28-L37), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L41-L46)

The column schema is grouped into identity, outcome, split-group, condition, missing-state, nucleic-acid, and link families.
