The discrete variant additionally accepts normalized float timesteps in `[0, 1]` and quantizes them to table indices via `_time_to_index`, which is necessary because the discrete sampler expresses time as a continuous fraction ([protein_diffusion_model.py#L284-L300](/Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L284-L300)).

Sources: [unet_conditional_model.py](/ldm/unet_conditional_model.py#L21-L40), [protein_diffusion_model.py](/Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L284-L300)

## Triple-Condition Injection in the Residual Block

The `ResBlock` is where all three conditioning signals meet the sequence representation. The pattern is a lightweight, additive analogue of FiLM: each embedding is projected from `tdim` to the block's output width through its own `Swish → Linear` MLP, then broadcast across the length axis via `[:, :, None]` and **added** to the post-convolution feature map:

```python
h = self.block1(x)                      # GroupNorm → Swish → Conv1d(k=3)
h += self.temb_proj(temb)[:, :, None]   # timestep, broadcast over L
h += self.cemb_proj(cemb)[:, :, None]   # condition vector
h += self.yemb_proj(yemb)[:, :, None]   # phase label
h = self.block2(h) + self.shortcut(x)   # GroupNorm → Swish → Dropout → Conv1d, residual
return self.attn(h)
```

Sources: [unet_conditional_model.py](/ldm/unet_conditional_model.py#L112-L138)

Because the projection is per-channel (not per-position), conditioning acts as a **global, sequence-wide modulation**: the label and condition vectors bias which residue patterns the block favors, without distorting positional structure. The `shortcut` is a 1×1 convolution only when channel widths differ (`nn.Identity()` otherwise), and the optional trailing `AttnBlock` applies residual self-attention over the length axis: `GroupNorm(32)` → 1×1-conv Q/K/V projections → scaled dot-product attention (`w = bmm(q, k) * C^-0.5` → softmax → `bmm(w, v)`) → additive residual. This gives every block cheap access to long-range residue correlations that strided convolutions cannot express ([unet_conditional_model.py#L91-L109](/ldm/unet_conditional_model.py#L91-L109)).

> [!TIP]
> The discrete variant hardens this pattern for production: its `_squeeze_embedding` helper accepts embeddings as `[B, tdim]`, `[B, 1, tdim]`, or `None` (falling back to additive zero), and its GroupNorm uses `min(8, in_ch)` groups instead of a fixed 32 — so small channel widths (e.g. `ch=8` at the stem) do not crash GroupNorm's group-count constraint. When porting blocks between variants, these defensive defaults are the ones to carry over ([protein_diffusion_model.py#L156-L214](/Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L156-L214)).

Sources: [unet_conditional_model.py](/ldm/unet_conditional_model.py#L91-L109), [protein_diffusion_model.py](/Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L172-L214)

## Continuous vs Discrete I/O Contract

The head and tail conventions encode the diffusion regime. In the **continuous** variants, the head expands a single input channel to `ch` (`Conv1d(1, ch, 3)`) — in `ldm/unet_conditional_model.py` the `unsqueeze(1)` happens *inside* `forward`, whereas the minimal variant expects the caller to deliver `[B, 1, L]` already. The tail projects back to one channel; the canonical variant squeezes to `[B, L]`, the minimal variant returns `[B, 1, L]` and leaves squeezing to the trainer, which computes MSE against noise reshaped identically ([unet_conditional_model.py#L183-L202](/ldm/unet_conditional_model.py#L183-L202), [gaussian_diffusion.py#L30-L31](/ldm/ldm_minimal/diffusion/gaussian_diffusion.py#L30-L31)).

In the **discrete** variant, the head is preceded by a token embedding: `nn.Embedding(num_classes=21, ch)` maps amino-acid indices to dense vectors, permuted to `[B, ch, L]` before the convolutional stem (`Conv1d(ch, ch, 3)`). The tail emits `num_classes` logits per position, and `forward` returns `[B, L, num_classes]` after a final permute — exactly the shape cross-entropy losses and DDIM sampling consume ([protein_diffusion_model.py#L238-L242](/Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L238-L242), [protein_diffusion_model.py#L365-L367](/Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L365-L367)). The underlying diffusion wrapper (`ProteinDiffusionModel`) treats this UNet purely as a denoiser network and layers marginal transition matrices and a cosine noise schedule on top — those mechanics belong to [Marginal Transition Matrices](15-marginal-transition-matrices) and [Discrete Diffusion Foundations](14-discrete-diffusion-foundations).

| Contract element | Continuous (Gaussian) | Discrete (token) |
|---|---|---|
| Stem | `Conv1d(1 → ch)` on scalar signal | `nn.Embedding(21 → ch)` + `Conv1d(ch → ch)` |
| Tail | `Conv1d(ch → 1)` | `Conv1d(ch → num_classes)` |
| Output semantics | ε̂, regressed against sampled Gaussian noise (MSE) | Class logits per residue (CE) |
| Downstream loss site | `GaussianDiffusionTrainer.forward` | `ProteinDiffusionModel` loss + `Evaluator` recovery/perplexity |
| Timestep form | Long indices into the embedding table | Long indices **or** float `[0,1]` (auto-quantized) |

Sources: [unet_conditional_model.py](/ldm/unet_conditional_model.py#L183-L202), [protein_diffusion_model.py](/Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L302-L367), [gaussian_diffusion.py](/ldm/ldm_minimal/diffusion/gaussian_diffusion.py#L25-L32)

## The Classifier-Free Guidance Interface

All three denoisers expose the same four-argument signature — `forward(x, t, c, y)` — precisely so the diffusion wrappers can perform **classifier-free guidance** with two forward passes per sampling step: one conditioned on the real label, one on a null label. The samplers then extrapolate: `eps = (1 + w) * eps_cond − w * eps_uncond`, where the unconditional pass substitutes `torch.zeros_like(labels)` (canonical) or `torch.zeros_like(y)` (minimal). The guidance weight comes from configuration (`args.dif_w` in `ldm/diffusion_utils.py`, default `w=0.5` in the minimal sampler).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["x_t, t, c, y"] --> B["eps_cond = model(x_t, t, c, y)"]
    A --> C["null labels = zeros_like(y)"]
    C --> D["eps_uncond = model(x_t, t, c, 0)"]
    B --> E["eps = (1+w)·eps_cond − w·eps_uncond"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["x_{t-1} = coeff1·x_t − coeff2·eps + √var·noise"]
    F -->|"loop t = T-1 … 0"| A
    F --> G["clip to [-1, 1] → x_0"]
```

Training complements this with **label dropout**: `ldm/training.py` zeroes the labels with 10% probability per batch (`if np.random.rand() < 0.1`), teaching the network the unconditional distribution that CFG later extrapolates from ([training.py#L26-L30](/ldm/training.py#L26-L30)). The loss is reduced as `loss.sum() / B²`, a per-element normalization that keeps gradient scale stable across batch sizes ([training.py#L33-L35](/ldm/training.py#L33-L35)). The discrete pipeline goes further at inference: validation runs MC-dropout DDIM sampling ensembles (`ensemble_num=50`, `ddim_steps=50`) and averages the logit ensembles before computing recovery and perplexity — the UNet's dropout layers double as a Bayesian uncertainty source ([training.py#L139-L178](/Discrete/training.py#L139-L178)).

> [!TIP]
> Watch the positional argument order when wiring a trainer to a denoiser. `ldm/ldm_minimal/diffusion/gaussian_diffusion.py` calls `self.model(x_t.unsqueeze(1), t, c, y)` — condition vector third, matching the UNet signature — while `ldm/diffusion_utils.py` calls `self.model(x_t, t, labels, cond)`, passing the label as the third positional argument. With the canonical `LabelEmbedding` being a `Linear(1, dim)` on a float view and `ConditionEmbedding` being `Linear(input_dim, dim)`, swapping these two arguments silently changes which embedding head receives the 14-dim condition vector versus the scalar label. Verify `forward` order against the caller before reusing either diffusion wrapper ([diffusion_utils.py#L26-L37](/ldm/diffusion_utils.py#L26-L37), [gaussian_diffusion.py#L30](/ldm/ldm_minimal/diffusion/gaussian_diffusion.py#L30)).

Sources: [diffusion_utils.py](/ldm/diffusion_utils.py#L40-L88), [gaussian_diffusion.py](/ldm/ldm_minimal/diffusion/gaussian_diffusion.py#L53-L73), [training.py](/ldm/training.py#L26-L35)

## Constructor Surface

All variants expose a small, uniform configuration surface; `tdim` is always derived as `ch * 4`, so the embedding width scales automatically with the channel budget.

| Parameter | Meaning | Notes / defaults |
|---|---|---|
| `T` | Number of diffusion timesteps | Sizes the `TimeEmbedding` lookup table; must match the wrapper's schedule (`dif_T` at training time) |
| `ch` | Base channel width | Also drives embedding width `tdim = ch * 4` |
| `ch_mult` | Channel pyramid, e.g. `[1, 2, 4]` | Length is halved at each interior level via `DownSample` |
| `num_res_blocks` | ResBlocks per level (down path) | Up path uses `num_res_blocks + 1` to absorb skip concatenations |
| `dropout` | Dropout inside `block2` of every ResBlock | Also serves MC-dropout sampling in the discrete pipeline |
| `condition_dim` / `cond_dim` | Width of the condition vector | Default `14` in both minimal and discrete variants; matches `(B, 14)` batches in the minimal trainer |
| `num_classes` | Label/输出 vocabulary size | `2` (binary phase label) minimal; `21` (amino acids) discrete; controls token embedding and tail width |

Sources: [unet_conditional_model.py](/ldm/unet_conditional_model.py#L141-L148), [unet_denoising_esmc.py](/ldm/ldm_minimal/diffusion/unet_denoising_esmc.py#L144-L150), [protein_diffusion_model.py](/Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L220-L236), [training.py](/ldm/ldm_minimal/diffusion/training.py#L26-L35)

One integration note: the end-to-end latent pipeline mixes the diffusion loss into a composite objective — cross-entropy on reconstructed tokens (with token 21 down-weighted to 0.8), an L2 penalty on the latent representation, and the diffusion term — before the UNet's noise prediction ever sees the sequence directly ([losses.py#L8-L41](/ldm/utils/losses.py#L8-L41)). How the JTAE compressor produces the latent sequence that the continuous denoiser then diffuses is the subject of [Latent Diffusion with JTAE](17-latent-diffusion-with-jtae).

Sources: [losses.py](/ldm/utils/losses.py#L8-L41)

## Where This Fits — and Where to Go Next

Within the Generative Models track, this page is the network-level deep dive: upstream, [Discrete Diffusion Foundations](14-discrete-diffusion-foundations) and [Marginal Transition Matrices](15-marginal-transition-matrices) define the corruption process the discrete UNet inverts; downstream, [Latent Diffusion with JTAE](17-latent-diffusion-with-jtae) wraps the continuous variant inside a compressed latent space, and [Sequence Generation Evaluation](18-sequence-generation-evaluation) measures what the denoiser's sampled outputs are worth (recovery, perplexity — the exact metrics the discrete `Trainer` optimizes model selection against). If your goal is to reuse the denoiser in a new pipeline, start from the minimal variant (`ldm/ldm_minimal/`) — its trainer/sampler pair has the cleanest positional-argument contract — and carry over the discrete variant's defensive embedding handling only when your inputs can be missing or variable-shaped.


# Latent Diffusion with JTAE



This page documents the `ldm/` module of OpenPhase: a latent diffusion system in which a **Joint Transformer AutoEncoder (JTAE)** compresses protein sequences into compact continuous vectors, and a conditional Gaussian diffusion model learns to generate those vectors directly in latent space. Unlike the discrete token-space diffusion covered in [Discrete Diffusion Foundations](14-discrete-diffusion-foundations), here the diffusion process never touches token IDs — it operates entirely on the JTAE bottleneck output, while sequence reconstruction is handled by a convolutional decoder. We cover the encoder stack, the joint training objective, the latent-space diffusion trainer/sampler, the conditional UNet denoiser specialized for latent vectors, and the two available implementations (token-level and minimal embedding-level).

Sources: [jtae_.py](ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py#L1-L152), [diffusion_utils.py](ldm/diffusion_utils.py#L1-L90)

## Why Latent Diffusion

The core architectural decision is to factor generation into two cooperating components. The **JTAE** learns a bijective-ish mapping between a full-length token sequence and a single `latent_dim`-sized vector, while a **Gaussian diffusion model** learns the distribution of those vectors conditioned on labels and condition vectors. This design trades off against the discrete-diffusion pipeline in two ways: the diffusion model's denoising target is a short continuous vector rather than a full token grid, and reconstruction quality is owned by the autoencoder rather than by the diffusion step itself. Notably, both components are trained **jointly** in a single forward pass — the encoder, decoder, and latent diffusion share one optimizer step — rather than in the classic two-stage (autoencode-then-freeze) recipe.

The module's lineage is explicitly acknowledged: the bottleneck, decoder blocks, positional encoding, and loss function are adapted from the PRO-LDM repository, while the diffusion trainer and conditional UNet follow the ConDiff classifier-free-guidance design.

Sources: [jtae_.py](ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py#L84-L99), [bneck.py](ldm/JTAE/bneck.py#L3-L13), [losses.py](ldm/utils/losses.py#L5-L7)

## Architecture at a Glance

The following diagram shows the complete data flow through the system during a training forward pass. A token sequence `x` is embedded, encoded by a Performer attention network, pooled to a single vector via learned global attention, and compressed by a bottleneck. That latent vector `z_rep` feeds **two** paths simultaneously: the decoder (for reconstruction loss) and the Gaussian diffusion trainer (for latent-space denoising loss). Both losses are summed into one objective.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph JTAE["JTAE AutoEncoder (ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py)"]
        X["Token sequence x<br/>(B, seq_len)"] --> E["nn.Embedding<br/>(B, S, embedding_dim)"]
        E --> PE["PositionalEncoding<br/>(sinusoidal)"]
        PE --> PF["Performer encoder<br/>(causal linear attention)"]
        PF --> GA["Global attention pooling<br/>Linear(E,1) + Softmax + bmm"]
        GA --> BN["BaseBottleneck<br/>Linear + ReLU → (B, latent_dim)"]
        BN --> Z["z_rep"]
    end

    Z -->|"decode"| DEC["Conv decoder<br/>Linear → reshape → ResBlock → Conv1d"]
    DEC --> XHAT["x_hat logits<br/>(B, input_dim, seq_len)"]
    Z -->|"unsqueeze → (B,1,latent)"| DIF["GaussianDiffusionTrainer<br/>+ conditional UNet"]
    DIF --> DLOSS["diff_loss"]
    XHAT --> L["loss_function<br/>CE + L2(z) + σ·diff_loss"]
    DLOSS --> L
    X -->|"targets"| L

    style Z fill:#e8eaf6,stroke:#3f51b5
    style L fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#ef6c00
```

The key structural fact: the diffused object is a **single vector per sample**. The UNet receives it as a length-1 sequence (`z_rep.unsqueeze(1)`), so the entire U-Net hierarchy operates on `(B, 1, latent_dim)` tensors rather than the `(B, seq_len, vocab)` grids used by token-space diffusion.

Sources: [jtae_.py](ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py#L146-L152), [unet_conditional_model.py](ldm/unet_conditional_model.py#L141-L200)

## The JTAE Encoder Stack

Encoding proceeds through five stages, each with a precise shape contract. First, token IDs are mapped into an `embedding_dim`-sized space via `nn.Embedding`. Second, sinusoidal positional encodings are added so the permutation-invariant attention can recover residue order — the encoding buffer follows the standard `sin/cos` formulation with a 10000.0 wavelength base and is registered as a non-persistent buffer (not saved in checkpoints). Third, a **Performer** encoder with causal linear attention (4 heads by default, `layers` depth, `probs` dropout on both feed-forward and attention) produces contextualized residue representations.

Fourth — and this is the pivotal design point — a learned **global attention pooling** collapses the whole sequence into one vector: a `Linear(embedding_dim, 1)` + `Softmax(dim=1)` head produces per-residue weights `(B, S, 1)`, and a batched matrix multiply computes the weighted sum, yielding `(B, embedding_dim)`. Finally, the `BaseBottleneck` applies `Linear(embedding_dim, latent_dim)` followed by ReLU, producing the non-negative latent vector that diffusion will model.

| Stage | Module | Input → Output shape | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Token embedding | `nn.Embedding` | `(B, S)` → `(B, S, E)` | `input_dim` classes |
| Positional encoding | `PositionalEncoding` | `(B, S, E)` → `(B, S, E)` | Sinusoidal, `max_len=seq_len` |
| Contextual encoding | `Performer` | `(B, S, E)` → `(B, S, E)` | Causal, 4 heads, dropout `probs` |
| Global pooling | `Linear(E,1)+Softmax` + `bmm` | `(B, S, E)` → `(B, E)` | Learned per-residue weights |
| Bottleneck | `BaseBottleneck` | `(B, E)` → `(B, latent_dim)` | Linear + ReLU |

Sources: [jtae_.py](ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py#L53-L79), [jtae_.py](ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py#L108-L128), [positionalencoding.py](ldm/JTAE/positionalencoding.py#L12-L32), [bneck.py](ldm/JTAE/bneck.py#L6-L13)

> [!TIP]
> The global-attention pooling at [jtae_.py](ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py#L118-L128) is what makes the latent diffusion tractable at all: because the sequence is reduced to one vector **before** the bottleneck, the diffusion UNet never has to denoise a `seq_len × vocab` tensor. If you adapt this code to longer sequences or larger latent grids, the UNet channel budget in `dif_channel_mult` — not the encoder — becomes the bottleneck.

## The Convolutional Decoder

Decoding inverts the compression geometrically rather than autoregressively. The latent vector is first projected by a linear layer to `seq_len × (hidden_dim // 2)` values, then reshaped into `(B, hidden_dim // 2, seq_len)` — this reshape happens at index 1 of the decoder `ModuleList`. A residual 1D convolution `Block` (two 3-kernel convolutions with BatchNorm, plus a 1×1 skip projection when channel counts differ) expands to `hidden_dim` channels, and a final `Conv1d(hidden_dim, input_dim, kernel_size=3, padding=1)` emits per-position logits over the full token vocabulary.

The residual `Block` is adapted from PRO-LDM and uses an explicit `use_skip` flag: the skip path activates only when `stride != 1` or channel counts mismatch, otherwise it is an `nn.Identity`. The decoder's output is consumed as classification logits — reconstruction quality is measured by cross-entropy against token IDs, not by continuous regression.

Sources: [jtae_.py](ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py#L101-L136), [convolution.py](ldm/JTAE/convolution.py#L10-L42)

## Joint Training Objective

The complete loss is assembled in `loss_function` and combines three weighted terms:

- **Reconstruction** (`ae_loss`): weighted cross-entropy between decoder logits `(B, input_dim, seq_len)` and token targets, with the token class at index 21 downweighted to 0.8 (a vocabulary-specific adjustment) and the whole term scaled by `gamma_val`.
- **Latent regularization** (`zrep_l2_loss`): `0.5 · mean(‖z_rep‖₂²)` scaled by `eta_val` — this shrinks the latent geometry that the diffusion model must fit.
- **Latent diffusion** (`diff_loss`): the MSE denoising loss from the Gaussian trainer, scaled by `sigma_val`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph FWD["jtae.forward(x, y, c)"]
        A["encode(x) → z (B, latent_dim)"] --> B["unsqueeze → (B,1,latent_dim)"]
        B --> C["diff_train(z, y, c)<br/>10% label dropout → CFG"]
        C --> D["diff_loss · Σ/b²"]
        B --> E["squeeze → decode(z)<br/>x_hat (B, input_dim, S)"]
    end
    D --> F["loss_function:<br/>γ·CE(x_hat, x) + η·½‖z‖² + σ·diff_loss"]
    E --> F
```

Two mechanics deserve attention. First, **the label-dropout trick for classifier-free guidance is embedded inside `diff_train` itself**: with probability 0.1 per batch, labels are zeroed before the diffusion trainer is invoked, teaching the UNet both a conditional and an unconditional denoising direction. Second, the diffusion loss is normalized as `loss.sum() / (b ** 2)` — sum-then-divide-by-batch-squared — matching the PRO-LDM convention, so the effective per-element scale shrinks as batch size grows. A diagnostic, `seq_difference` (fraction of positions where `argmax(x_hat)` disagrees with the target), is logged to W&B alongside the three loss components.

Sources: [losses.py](ldm/utils/losses.py#L8-L54), [jtae_.py](ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py#L138-L152)

> [!TIP]
> Because encoder, decoder, and diffusion model are optimized in **one** step, the loss weights `gamma_val`, `eta_val`, and `sigma_val` are a three-way tug-of-war over the latent space: raising `sigma_val` pressures `z_rep` toward the diffusion model's preferred distribution, while raising `gamma_val` pressures it toward reconstruction fidelity. When generation quality degrades, tune this triple before touching diffusion-side hyperparameters.

## Diffusion in Latent Space: Trainer and Sampler

The diffusion machinery in [diffusion_utils.py](ldm/diffusion_utils.py) implements the standard DDPM pair of algorithms with a **linear** beta schedule interpolated from `dif_beta_1` to `dif_beta_T` across `dif_T` steps. The trainer samples `t` uniformly per example, constructs `x_t = √ᾱ_t · x_0 + √(1−ᾱ_t) · ε`, predicts the noise `ε` through the conditional UNet, and returns element-wise MSE. Coefficients are stored as registered buffers (`sqrt_alphas_bar`, `sqrt_one_minus_alphas_bar`) in double precision.

The sampler implements Algorithm 2 (reverse process) with **classifier-free guidance extrapolation** at every step: it runs the UNet twice — once with the true label and once with zeroed labels — and combines them as `ε = (1+w)·ε_cond − w·ε_null`, where `w = args.dif_w`. It then steps backward through the posterior mean/variance formulation for `T` iterations and clips the final latent to `[-1, 1]`. During generation, this clipped latent `z̃` replaces `z_rep` as decoder input to synthesize sequences.

| Aspect | Trainer | Sampler |
|---|---|---|
| Schedule | Linear betas `β₁→β_T`, cumulative `ᾱ` | Same buffers + posterior variance |
| Input | Clean latent `z` + labels + condition | Pure noise `x_T` + labels + condition |
| Guidance | 10% label dropout (in `diff_train`) | Extrapolation `(1+w)·ε_cond − w·ε_null` |
| Output | Element-wise MSE loss | Latent `x_0` clipped to `[-1, 1]` |

Sources: [diffusion_utils.py](ldm/diffusion_utils.py#L14-L88), [jtae_.py](ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py#L138-L144)

## The Conditional UNet for Latents

The denoiser in [unet_conditional_model.py](ldm/unet_conditional_model.py) is a 1D U-Net purpose-built for latent vectors: the stem is `Conv1d(1, ch)`, treating the `latent_dim` vector as a single-position sequence, and the tail projects back to one channel. It fuses **three** conditioning signals into every residual block via additive projections: a sinusoidal **time embedding** (`TimeEmbedding`: `T`-sized lookup table → 2-layer MLP), a **continuous condition embedding** (`ConditionEmbedding`: MLP over the condition vector `c`), and a **label embedding** (`LabelEmbedding`: MLP over the scalar label viewed as `(B, 1)` float). Each `ResBlock` computes `h += temb_proj(t)[:,:,None] + cemb_proj(c)[:,:,None] + yemb_proj(y)[:,:,None]` between its two conv stacks.

The topology is conventional but attention-heavy: each resolution level contributes `num_res_blocks` ResBlocks in the down path with strided `DownSample` between levels, the bottleneck carries two ResBlocks both with self-attention (`AttnBlock`: GroupNorm + single-head scaled dot-product over the length-1 axis), and the up path uses `num_res_blocks + 1` blocks with skip concatenation and transposed-conv `UpSample`. Note the input channel arithmetic: `ResBlock`s in the up path receive `chs.pop() + now_ch` channels, wiring every encoder feature map into its decoder counterpart.

Sources: [unet_conditional_model.py](ldm/unet_conditional_model.py#L21-L66), [unet_conditional_model.py](ldm/unet_conditional_model.py#L112-L138), [unet_conditional_model.py](ldm/unet_conditional_model.py#L141-L203)

## Two Implementations: Token-Level vs. Minimal

The repository ships two JTAE variants for different input regimes. The full version in `ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py` consumes **token IDs** and owns the entire embedding pipeline (lookup table → positional encoding → Performer). The minimal version in `ldm/ldm_minimal/JTAE_minimal.py` assumes you arrive with **pre-computed residue embeddings** (e.g., language-model outputs): it concatenates the protein embedding `x` with the condition vector `c` into a single `input_dim = D_x + D_c` vector, then uses plain linear layers for embedding and bottleneck — no attention at all. The decoder stacks and diffusion trainers are structurally identical between the two.

| Dimension | `ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py` (full) | `ldm/ldm_minimal/JTAE_minimal.py` (minimal) |
|---|---|---|
| Input | Token IDs `(B, S)` | Fused ESM + condition `(B, D_x + D_c)` |
| Token embedding | `nn.Embedding` | `nn.Linear` over concatenated features |
| Sequence context | Performer (causal, multi-layer) | None (order handled upstream by ESM) |
| Pooling | Global attention + bottleneck | Single linear bottleneck |
| Batch interface | `forward(x, y, c)` tuple | `forward_dict({x, c, y})` |
| Guidance dropout | In-model, `np.random.rand() < 0.1` | In-model, `torch.rand < 0.1`, labels cast `.long()` |
| External deps | `performer_pytorch`, ConDiff | ConDiff (DiffusionFreeGuidence) |

Sources: [jtae_.py](ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py#L53-L99), [JTAE_minimal.py](ldm/ldm_minimal/JTAE_minimal.py#L23-L85)

## Training Loop and Optimization Setup

The reference driver in [utils/training.py](ldm/utils/training.py) wires everything together with W&B project tracking (`Open-Phase`), an h5ad data source split 90/10 with seed 42, and per-batch steps of: `zero_grad → forward(x, c, y) → loss_function → backward → step`. Checkpointing saves model/optimizer/scheduler state plus the full `args` namespace every 50 epochs and at the final epoch, and resume support restores all three states from disk.

Optimization uses **AdamW** (lr `2e-5`, weight decay `1e-4`) under a composite schedule: a custom `GradualWarmupScheduler` ramps the learning rate linearly to `multiplier × base_lr` over `n_epochs // 10` epochs, then hands off to `CosineAnnealingLR` decayed to zero. The default model geometry is substantial — `embedding_dim` 512, `hidden_dim` 512, `latent_dim` 256, `seq_len` 2048 — and the diffusion defaults are `T=1000` steps, base channels 64 with multipliers `[1, 2, 4]`, 2 residual blocks per level, dropout 0.15, and betas from `1e-4` to `0.028`.

| Hyperparameter group | Defaults (argparse) |
|---|---|
| Autoencoder | `input_dim=1152`, `embedding_dim=512`, `hidden_dim=512`, `latent_dim=256`, `seq_len=2048`, `layers=4`, `probs=0.2` |
| Objective weights | `gamma_val=1.0`, `eta_val=0.001`, `sigma_val=1.5` |
| Diffusion | `dif_T=1000`, `dif_channel=64`, `dif_channel_mult=[1,2,4]`, `dif_res_blocks=2`, `dif_dropout=0.15`, `dif_beta_1=1e-4`, `dif_beta_T=0.028` |
| Optimization | `lr=2e-5`, `batch_size=8`, `n_epochs=100`, warmup multiplier `2.5` |

Sources: [utils/training.py](ldm/utils/training.py#L53-L175), [utils/scheduler.py](ldm/utils/scheduler.py#L4-L31)

## Module Map and Code Organization

The `ldm/` tree contains some deliberate duplication worth knowing about before you edit. `ldm/Scheduler.py` and `ldm/utils/scheduler.py` are identical copies of `GradualWarmupScheduler`; `ldm/bneck.py` and `ldm/convolution.py` are dict-batch-flavored variants (they unpack a `batch['x']` key) of the JTAE tensor-flavored originals. The file `ldm/training.py` is a standalone per-batch diffusion training function that trains the UNet directly on a batch's `x_0` — including the same 10% label-dropout and `Σ/b²` normalization — useful when you want to fine-tune the denoiser without the autoencoder in the loop.

| File | Role | Reuse note |
|---|---|---|
| `ldm/JTAE/jtae_.py` | Full token-level JTAE + embedded diffusion | Primary model |
| `ldm/JTAE/{bneck,convolution,positionalencoding}.py` | Encoder/decoder building blocks | Adapted from PRO-LDM |
| `ldm/diffusion_utils.py` | DDPM trainer + CFG sampler | Shared by both variants |
| `ldm/unet_conditional_model.py` | Triple-conditioned 1D UNet | Latent-space denoiser |
| `ldm/utils/{losses,training,scheduler}.py` | Objective, driver, LR schedule | Canonical versions |
| `ldm/training.py` | Standalone diffusion-only train step | Fine-tuning path |
| `ldm/Scheduler.py`, `ldm/bneck.py`, `ldm/convolution.py` | Duplicates / dict-batch variants | Prefer `utils/` + `JTAE/` originals |
| `ldm/ldm_minimal/JTAE_minimal.py` | ESM-embedding-level variant | No attention encoder |

Sources: [Scheduler.py](ldm/Scheduler.py#L1-L32), [utils/scheduler.py](ldm/utils/scheduler.py#L1-L32), [bneck.py](ldm/bneck.py#L1-L21), [convolution.py](ldm/convolution.py#L1-L50), [training.py](ldm/training.py#L6-L36)

## Where This Fits and What to Read Next

Conceptually, this page sits between the token-space diffusion stack and evaluation: the discrete pipeline denoises sequences position-by-position (see [Marginal Transition Matrices](15-marginal-transition-matrices) and [Conditional UNet Denoiser](16-conditional-unet-denoiser) for that contrast), whereas this latent pipeline denoises a pooled sequence summary and delegates token-level fidelity to the decoder. To measure whether latent-space generation produces viable proteins, continue to [Sequence Generation Evaluation](18-sequence-generation-evaluation); to understand where the condition vectors `c` consumed by the UNet come from, see [Condition Feature Engineering](13-condition-feature-engineering); and for the full grid of tunable parameters referenced above, consult the [Hyperparameter Grid Reference](22-hyperparameter-grid-reference).


# Sequence Generation Evaluation



Generated protein sequences are only as useful as our ability to score them. This page documents OpenPhase's discrete-diffusion evaluation subsystem: the `Evaluator` class that computes recovery, BLOSUM-based substitution scores, and perplexity; the tensor-to-string decoding layer that bridges model output to human-readable sequences; and the validation/test protocols embedded in `Trainer` that turn raw scores into model selection decisions. A generated sequence is scored against its paired ground-truth target along two axes — exact positional agreement and biochemical substitution plausibility — under both stochastic (validation) and deterministic (test) decoding regimes.

Sources: [evaluator.py](Discrete/evaluator.py#L1-L45), [training.py](Discrete/training.py#L62-L83)

## Evaluation Pipeline Architecture

The evaluation subsystem is a three-module pipeline with a strictly typed interface contract. The sampler (`ProteinDiffusionModel.mc_ddim_sample`) produces a three-element tuple — fused logits, one-hot sequences, and decoded strings. The decode layer (`tensor_to_sequence_list`) performs argmax over the 21-class vocabulary and maps indices to amino acid characters. The `Evaluator` consumes index tensors directly from the sampler's argmax outputs and the fused logits, producing the final metric suite. This separation means the metrics are sampler-agnostic: any component emitting `(logits [B, L, 21], onehot [B, L, 21], seqs [list[str]])` can be evaluated without modification.

Sources: [protein_diffusion_model.py](Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L530-L571), [tensor_to_list.py](Discrete/tensor_to_list.py#L6-L22), [evaluator.py](Discrete/evaluator.py#L5-L21)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Sampler["ProteinDiffusionModel.mc_ddim_sample"]
        ZT["z_T sampled from stationary marginal"] --> DDIM["DDIM denoising loop<br/>with ESM2-650M prior fusion"]
        DDIM --> OUT["(last_logits, final_onehot, seqs)"]
    end
    subgraph Decode["tensor_to_list.py decode layer"]
        OUT --> ARG["argmax dim=-1 to token indices [B, L]"]
        ARG --> STR["IDX_TO_AA lookup to sequence strings"]
    end
    subgraph Eval["Evaluator"]
        BLOSUM["eval_blosums.pth<br/>BLOSUM45/62/80/90"]
        REC["cal_recovery"]
        NSSR["cal_all_blosum_nssr"]
        PPL["cal_perplexity"]
        BLOSUM --> NSSR
    end
    OUT --> PPL
    ARG --> REC
    ARG --> NSSR
    REC --> SEL["Trainer.validate()<br/>best-model selection"]
    PPL --> SEL
    REC --> TST["Trainer.test()<br/>final report dict"]
    NSSR --> TST
    PPL --> TST
```

A subtle but important interface detail: in `Trainer.validate()` and `Trainer.test()`, the ground-truth tensor `x` passed to `mc_ddim_sample` acts only as a **batch shape template** — the sampler initializes from the stationary marginal distribution and conditions generation on `c` alone; `x` is never consulted inside the denoising step. Evaluation therefore measures *conditional generation from the condition vector* scored against the paired target, with sequence length inherited from the target. The returned string list `seqs` is produced by the sampler but unused by the Trainer, leaving a clean hook for downstream string-level analyses (e.g., export or external property predictors).

Sources: [protein_diffusion_model.py](Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L534-L544), [protein_diffusion_model.py](Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L576-L601), [training.py](Discrete/training.py#L153-L166)

## The Evaluator Class: Metric Implementations

`Evaluator` is a plain object (no nn.Module dependency) constructed around a precomputed BLOSUM archive. On init, it loads `eval_blosums.pth` — a dictionary of four 20×20 substitution matrices keyed by `BLOSUM45`, `BLOSUM62`, `BLOSUM80`, `BLOSUM90` — and records the canonical BLOSUM axis order (`A, R, N, D, C, Q, E, G, H, I, L, K, M, F, P, S, T, W, Y, V`). An optional reordering mechanism permutes matrix rows and columns via `np.ix_` so that lookups can follow a caller-supplied amino acid ordering instead.

Sources: [evaluator.py](Discrete/evaluator.py#L5-L21), [evaluator.py](Discrete/evaluator.py#L13-L21)

The complete metric API is intentionally minimal — four methods, all stateless with respect to batches:

| Method | Inputs | Computation | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cal_recovery` | `pred_seq [L]`, `target_seq [L]` index tensors | elementwise equality, meaned | scalar in [0, 1] |
| `cal_blosum_nssr` | `pred_seq`, `target_seq`, `blosum_name` | fraction of positions where `blosum[pred, target] > 0` | scalar in [0, 1] |
| `cal_all_blosum_nssr` | `pred_seq`, `target_seq` | applies `cal_blosum_nssr` across all four matrices, ordered 45→62→80→90 | list of 4 scalars |
| `cal_perplexity` | `pred_logits [N, 21]`, `target_label [N]` | `exp(mean cross-entropy)` | scalar ≥ 1 |

Sources: [evaluator.py](Discrete/evaluator.py#L23-L45)

**Recovery** (also called sequence recovery or AAR in the protein-design literature) is the strictest positional metric: a predicted token must match the target exactly. **NSSR** (normalized substitution score ratio) relaxes this to *biochemically plausible* agreement — any substitution with a positive BLOSUM score counts as a hit, rewarding conservative mutations like I↔V or D↔E while penalizing radical ones. **Perplexity** operates at a different abstraction level entirely: rather than scoring a decoded sequence, it measures the calibrated sharpness of the full predictive distribution, computed as the exponential of the mean cross-entropy between fused ensemble logits and target labels across all positions of the evaluation set simultaneously.

Sources: [evaluator.py](Discrete/evaluator.py#L23-L26), [evaluator.py](Discrete/evaluator.py#L35-L39), [evaluator.py](Discrete/evaluator.py#L41-L45)

## Sequence Decoding and Alphabet Contract

The decode layer defines the vocabulary contract shared by generation and evaluation: `IDX_TO_AA` maps indices 0–19 to the twenty standard amino acids in alphabetical order (A, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, N, P, Q, R, S, T, V, W, Y) and reserves index 20 for `X` (unknown). Decoding accepts a `[B, L, 21]` one-hot tensor, applies `argmax(dim=-1)`, and builds strings character-by-character — with one twist: positions flagged in an optional boolean `mask` render as `X` regardless of their argmax value, which is how the entropy-gated positions are surfaced to the ESM prior during sampling.

Sources: [tensor_to_list.py](Discrete/tensor_to_list.py#L1-L4), [tensor_to_list.py](Discrete/tensor_to_list.py#L6-L22)

The same utility serves three distinct call sites in the sampler: constructing masked inputs for the ESM prior during training loss computation, decoding the final denoised sequence in `mc_ddim_sample`, and producing per-step sequence strings inside the DDIM loop. Because `dataset.py` normalizes all stored data to long token indices (`[N, L]`) by pre-collapsing one-hot inputs, the evaluator consistently receives index tensors — never raw one-hot — which keeps `cal_recovery` and the BLOSUM lookups cheap.

Sources: [protein_diffusion_model.py](Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L492-L497), [protein_diffusion_model.py](Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L566-L569), [protein_diffusion_model.py](Discrete/protein_diffusion_model.py#L604-L613), [dataset.py](Discrete/dataset.py#L6-L12)

> [!TIP]
> The BLOSUM axis order recorded in `Evaluator` (`A, R, N, D, C, Q, ...`) is **not** the model's index order (`A, C, D, E, F, ...`). The `reorder_blosum`/`reorder_types` mechanism exists precisely to permute matrix axes into model index space via `np.ix_`, but it is disabled by default (`reorder_blosum=False`) — and `Trainer` instantiates `Evaluator()` with defaults. Before trusting NSSR numbers, verify which axis order `eval_blosums.pth` was saved in; if it uses the canonical BLOSUM order, pass `reorder_blosum=True, reorder_types=<your 20-AA index order>` at construction. Additionally, index 20 (`X`) has no row in a 20×20 BLOSUM matrix, so any generated sequence containing an `X` token will raise an indexing error in `cal_blosum_nssr` — strip or remap `X` positions before scoring.

## Validation Protocol: MC-Dropout Ensemble Scoring

Validation runs at a configurable cadence (`save_and_sample_every` epochs) and implements a three-stage ensemble protocol. First, the model is set to eval mode but dropout is explicitly re-enabled via `enable_dropout()`, converting the deterministic UNet into a stochastic ensemble member generator. Second, for each validation batch, the sampler executes `ensemble_num=50` independent `mc_ddim_sample` passes with `diverse=True` — multinomial sampling from the posterior — and the resulting logit stacks are averaged into `mean_logits`. Third, per-sample argmax of these mean logits is compared against targets for `cal_recovery`.

Sources: [training.py](Discrete/training.py#L139-L166), [utils_.py](Discrete/utils_.py#L142-L146)

Two design decisions in this protocol deserve attention. The **median** — not the mean — recovery is the selection statistic, retrieved via `cal_stats_metric` and tracked in `best_val_recovery`; medians are robust to sequences of anomalous length or degenerate generation, making model selection less sensitive to outlier batches. And perplexity is computed **globally**, over the concatenation of all batch logits and targets flattened to `[N·L, 21]` / `[N·L]`, rather than averaged per-batch — a single exp of a single mean cross-entropy over the entire validation corpus. When median recovery improves, the current model is deep-copied into `best_model` alongside its perplexity, epoch, and step stamps.

Sources: [training.py](Discrete/training.py#L168-L187), [utils_.py](Discrete/utils_.py#L135-L139)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["model.eval() + enable_dropout()"] --> B["iterate val_dataloader"]
    B --> C["run ensemble_num = 50<br/>mc_ddim_sample(diverse=True)"]
    C --> D["stack and mean logits"]
    D --> E["per-sample argmax to cal_recovery"]
    E --> B
    B --> F["concatenate all logits and targets"]
    F --> G["cal_perplexity over all positions"]
    G --> H["median recovery = selection statistic"]
    H --> I{"median_rec greater than best?"}
    I -->|yes| J["deepcopy best_model<br/>stamp ppl, epoch, step"]
    I -->|no| K["keep training"]
    J --> L["resume training loop"]
    K --> L
```

## Test Protocol: Deterministic Decoding and BLOSUM Scoring

Testing loads the deep-copied `best_model` and runs the same ensemble machinery with two decisive switches: dropout remains in eval mode (no MC sampling of the network itself), and `diverse=False` makes the DDIM posterior deterministic (argmax instead of multinomial). Per-sample scores now include the full BLOSUM ladder — `cal_all_blosum_nssr` unpacked into `n45`, `n62`, `n80`, `n90` lists — alongside recovery, with perplexity again computed over all concatenated positions.

Sources: [training.py](Discrete/training.py#L192-L225)

The final return dict is a deliberately compact summary: median and mean recovery, perplexity, and `mean_nssr62` only. The BLOSUM45/80/90 lists are computed per sample but never surfaced — neither in the return value nor in the `PrettyTable` report columns (which log only median recovery and perplexity). If your analysis depends on the full substitution-conservatism profile, you will need to either extend the return dict or invoke `Evaluator` directly outside the Trainer.

Sources: [training.py](Discrete/training.py#L230-L246), [training.py](Discrete/training.py#L81-L83)

| Aspect | `validate()` | `test()` |
|---|---|---|
| Model under evaluation | current training state | deep-copied `best_model` |
| Dropout | enabled (MC-Dropout members) | eval mode (deterministic) |
| Sampling mode | `diverse=True` (multinomial) | `diverse=False` (argmax) |
| Ensemble size | 50 averaged logit stacks | 50 averaged logit stacks |
| Recovery | per-sample, median = selector | per-sample, mean + median reported |
| BLOSUM NSSR | not computed | 4 matrices computed, only BLOSUM62 exported |
| Perplexity scope | all validation positions | all test positions |
| Output | updates `val_table`, `best_*` state | returns metrics dict |

## Interpreting the BLOSUM Ladder

The four matrices form a stringency ladder defined by the sequence-pair divergence they were derived from. Reading NSSR across the ladder tells you *how conservative* a generated substitution profile is, in a way raw recovery cannot:

| Matrix | Derived from pairs ≥ identity | Stringency | High NSSR implies |
|---|---|---|---|
| BLOSUM45 | 45% | loosest | only distant-homolog-level plausibility |
| BLOSUM62 | 62% | standard | conventional conservative substitutions |
| BLOSUM80 | 80% | strict | near-identical chemistry per position |
| BLOSUM90 | 90% | strictest | almost-exact positional agreement |

A generated sequence scoring high recovery but low BLOSUM90-NSSR is substituting aggressively while still landing exact matches frequently — typical of a model over-committed to mode-seeking. Conversely, high NSSR across all four matrices with moderate recovery indicates a model that reproduces the target's biochemical character even when tokens differ, which is often the more meaningful signal for functional-sequence generation.

Sources: [evaluator.py](Discrete/evaluator.py#L8-L10), [evaluator.py](Discrete/evaluator.py#L23-L33)

Note that perplexity and the positional metrics measure different failure modes and should never be traded off against each other implicitly: a model can achieve low perplexity (well-calibrated distributions) with poor recovery (wrong argmax), and vice versa. The Trainer's selection rule resolves this tension by anchoring solely on median recovery, with perplexity recorded as a diagnostic stamp on the selected checkpoint.

Sources: [training.py](Discrete/training.py#L171-L187)

## Integration Notes and Pitfalls

Three implementation details matter when wiring this evaluator into new pipelines. First, **portability**: `Evaluator.__init__` defaults `blosum_path` to an absolute path from the original author's machine, while the shipped archive lives at `Discrete/eval_blosums.pth` — instantiate with an explicit `blosum_path="Discrete/eval_blosums.pth"` (relative to your working directory) to avoid a `FileNotFoundError` at first use. Second, a legacy alternate recovery helper exists in `utils_.py` (`seq_recovery`) that compares one-hot tensors directly; it shares no call sites with the current Trainer and follows a different input contract (`data.x` one-hot vs. index tensors) — prefer the `Evaluator.cal_recovery` path for consistency. Third, results reporting is asymmetric by design: the `PrettyTable` logs capture recovery and perplexity only, so BLOSUM-based results depend on the test return dict.

Sources: [evaluator.py](Discrete/evaluator.py#L6-L14), [utils_.py](Discrete/utils_.py#L63-L70), [training.py](Discrete/training.py#L237-L246)

> [!TIP]
> `training.py` defines the `Trainer` class **twice** — the module re-imports its dependencies and re-declares an identical class starting around line 275. Python's last-definition-wins semantics mean the first definition is dead code at import time; any edits made to the first copy will silently never execute. Always modify the second (shadowing) definition, or consolidate to a single class before extending the evaluation protocols.

## Where to Go Next

This page covered the measurement layer; the quantities it consumes originate upstream in the generative stack. To understand where `mc_ddim_sample`'s fused logits come from — the conditional UNet predicting x₀ at each denoising step — continue with [Conditional UNet Denoiser](16-conditional-unet-denoiser). For the stationary marginal that initializes `z_T` and the transition matrices the DDIM posterior computation depends on, see [Marginal Transition Matrices](15-marginal-transition-matrices) and [Discrete Diffusion Foundations](14-discrete-diffusion-foundations). If your goal is comparing this evaluation protocol against the benchmark prediction baselines or dataset-level split metrics, the relevant context lives in [Outcome Prediction Baselines](8-outcome-prediction-baselines) and [Split Strategies and Metrics](10-split-strategies-and-metrics).

# Record Map Distance Model



Every dot in the Records Space explorer is one LLPS experiment record, and the model documented here is the reason any two dots sit near each other. The model defines a **weighted block distance** between records — protein, nucleic acid, physico-chemical conditions, buffer/additives — treats unreported values as a first-class state rather than imputing them, and derives four parallel "lens" geometries from it. Two implementations exist and must stay numerically identical: an offline NumPy engine (`colab/rslib.py`) that builds the precomputed 2-D maps, and a dependency-free browser reimplementation (`explorer/js/records_space.js`) that recomputes distances live for pasted experiments. This page dissects both, plus the calibration, diagnostics, and the approximation path for novel sequences.

Sources: [README.md](records_space/README.md#L9-L22), [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L1-L14), [records_space.js](records_space/explorer/js/records_space.js#L1-L2)

## Design Principles

Three commitments shape the whole model. First, a record is decomposed into blocks by data type — protein (sequence embedding), nucleic acid (mixed categorical/numeric), conditions (numeric), buffer/additives (sets) — and each block gets its own natural representation and distance before merging. Second, **readouts are never inputs**: labels, csat values, morphology, source, and paper are excluded from the geometry and only color the dots afterward, which keeps evaluation honest. Third, the weights and the missing-value penalty were fixed a priori and were **not tuned** — the README states this explicitly, so the geometry is a descriptive artifact, not an optimized classifier.

Sources: [README.md](records_space/README.md#L11-L21), [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L3-L13)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    R["Experiment record<br/>protein · nucleic acid · conditions · buffer<br/>(labels, csat, source excluded)"]
    R --> P["P · protein · w = 0.40<br/>ESMC-600M L18 → z-score → PCA(64) → cosine"]
    R --> N["N · nucleic acid · w = 0.15<br/>presence / class / names / length / conc / ratio / seq & fold"]
    R --> C["C · conditions · w = 0.35<br/>conc, pH, temp, salts, crowders"]
    R --> B["B · buffer & additives · w = 0.10<br/>multi-hot Jaccard"]
    P --> D["Weighted sum<br/>missing → λ = 0.5 (M+)<br/>or observed-only average (M−)"]
    N --> D
    C --> D
    B --> D
    D --> L1["full"]
    D --> L2["prot"]
    D --> L3["cond"]
    D --> L4["fullM"]
    L1 --> V["t-SNE / UMAP 2-D views<br/>+ kNN diagnostics"]
    L2 --> V
    L3 --> V
    L4 --> V
```

## The Four Distance Blocks

The block weights are constants of the model, mirrored in both the Python constants and the exported `params.json` consumed by the browser: `P=0.40, N=0.15, C=0.35, B=0.10`, with `λ=0.5` and a `temp_state_pen=0.2`. The final weighted sum divides by the total weight (1.0), so weights act directly as proportions.

| Block | Weight | Representation | Pairwise distance | Calibration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P — protein | 0.40 | ESMC-600M layer-18 residue mean (1,152-d) → z-score → PCA(64) → L2-normalize | cosine distance | divided by q95 of random-pair cosine distances |
| N — nucleic acid | 0.15 | presence/class (RNA=1/DNA=2), 13 name flags, log₁₀ length/conc/ratio, 4 sequence + 2 folding features | class indicator + name Jaccard + scaled \|Δ\| + scaled Euclidean | each sub-dimension scaled so random-pair q95 ≈ 1 |
| C — conditions | 0.35 | conc, pH, temp (range-scaled); salts, crowders (log₁₀(1+x), q95 of nonzero) | mean over 5 grouped dimensions, temp state penalty 0.2 | range: q95−q05 of observed; pos: q95 of nonzero |
| B — buffer/additives | 0.10 | multi-hot vectors: 8 buffer families, 12 additive families | Jaccard per set-dimension, averaged | none (set-based) |

Sources: [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L18-L26), [params.json](records_space/export/params.json#L2-L9), [README.md](records_space/README.md#L13-L18)

### Protein block (P)

`build_inputs` z-scores every ESMC dimension over the 1,338 unique dataset sequences, runs PCA to 64 components, subtracts the mean and L2-normalizes (`Zn`), then forms the full cosine distance matrix `1 − Zn·Znᵀ` clipped at zero. Records reference sequences by index (`pidx`; `pidx < 0` means no sequence). The raw cosine spread is recalibrated by `calibrate_P`, which samples 2,000,000 random sequence pairs and uses the 95th percentile of their distances as the divisor — the exported `scales.P = 1.3449` in `params.json` is exactly this value. Every block distance is also truncated to [0, 1].

Sources: [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L60-L78), [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L272-L281), [params.json](records_space/export/params.json#L28-L29)

### Nucleic acid block (N)

Seven dimensions are averaged: class mismatch (RNA vs DNA), name-class Jaccard over 13 flags (`polyU`, `tRNA`, `G4`, `ssDNA`, …), log₁₀-scaled length, concentration and NA:protein ratio (range-scaled over observed values), plus two vector dimensions — sequence features (GC content, purine fraction, log₁₀ longest homopolymer run, G4 flag) and folding features (MFE/nt, paired fraction). The two vector dimensions are z-scored and then globally rescaled so that the Euclidean distance between a random pair lands at the 95th-percentile ≈ 1, making them commensurate with the scalar dimensions. Crucially, "no nucleic acid" is a legal state, not missingness: present-vs-none contributes exactly 1.0 to the block, while numeric NA features of NA-free records are marked not-applicable rather than missing.

Sources: [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L99-L137), [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L228-L260)

### Conditions block (C)

Five grouped dimensions: protein concentration, pH, temperature, the salt group (MgCl₂/NaCl/KCl) and the crowder group (PEG1k/6k/20k, Ficoll, Dex40/70, Glycerol). Group members each contribute a scaled distance and the group sum is truncated to 1. Temperature carries a special **state penalty**: when one record reports a measured temperature and the other only "room temperature" (recorded as 22 °C), an extra `temp_state_pen = 0.2` is added on top of the numeric difference, encoding the provenance mismatch of the value itself.

Sources: [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L79-L98), [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L210-L225), [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L163-L172)

### Buffer and additives block (B)

Two Jaccard dimensions — buffer families (Tris, HEPES, phosphate, Good's MES, citrate, acetate, imidazole, other) and additive families (reducing agents, chelators, glycerol, nucleotides, denaturants, hexanediol, detergents, protein additives, polyanions, metals, dye probes, other) — averaged 50/50. Each set dimension independently tracks whether it was observed at all (`st_buffer`, `st_additive` states), feeding the missing-value policy below.

Sources: [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L138-L146), [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L263-L269)

## Missing Values as a State: M+ versus M−

The model's most distinctive choice is how it handles unreported dimensions. Instead of imputing, every scalar dimension returns three quantities: `d_plus` (the M+ distance), `d_obs` (observed-only distance), and coverage. The λ constant is deliberately set to 0.5 — half the typical (q95) separation — so a single missing dimension pushes records apart *moderately*: far enough to not fake agreement, near enough to not dominate the block.

| Situation | M+ (`full`, default) | M− (`fullM`) |
|---|---|---|
| both records observed | scaled \|Δ\| | scaled \|Δ\| |
| exactly one missing | λ = 0.5 | dimension excluded from the average |
| both missing | 0 | excluded |
| NA present vs none | 1.0 (hard rule, not missingness) | 1.0 |
| aggregation | fixed mean over all K dimensions | coverage-weighted mean over observed dimensions; 0.5 fallback if nothing observed |

Sources: [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L151-L160), [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L183-L191), [README.md](records_space/README.md#L20-L21)

> [!TIP]
> The `fullM` lens exists purely as a scientific control: comparing `full` against `fullM` layouts isolates how much of the map's structure is driven by the "missing-as-state" convention versus real reported values. The per-block coverage tensors (`cP, cN, cC, cB`) flow into `fullM`'s weighted average, so partial records never silently dominate.

## The Four Lenses

One chunked pass over the record table (`compute_lens_matrices`, 1,024 rows at a time, float32) emits all four N×N matrices simultaneously, reusing the per-block computations. Each lens answers a different question, and all four become selectable views in the explorer (`lens=tsne_full`, `umap_prot`, `umap_cond`, `umap_fullM`, …).

| Lens | Composition | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| `full` | 0.40·P + 0.15·N + 0.35·C + 0.10·B (M+) | the default, protein-centred map |
| `prot` | P alone | pure sequence neighbourhoods, no condition confound |
| `cond` | (0.15·N + 0.35·C + 0.10·B) / 0.60 | conditions and NA without any sequence signal |
| `fullM` | full with M− coverage-weighted averaging | sensitivity of the map to the missing-value convention |

Sources: [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L284-L310), [rs03_run.py](records_space/colab/rs03_run.py#L5-L9), [README.md](records_space/README.md#L54)

## Validating the Geometry

The model ships with three families of diagnostics rather than a train/test split, since it is descriptive.

**Condition coherence** (`rs07_coherence.py`) asks: do records that are 15-nearest neighbours in a lens actually have similar measured conditions? For each of four quantities — measured temperature (tolerance 2.0 °C), pH (0.2), NaCl (0.1 in log₁₀(1+mM)), protein concentration (0.2 in log₁₀ µM) — it computes the median |Δ| between neighbour pairs where *both* are observed, and compares against 400,000 random pairs from the same observed subset. This directly tests whether the C block's scaling produces real spatial coherence rather than artefacts.

Sources: [rs07_coherence.py](records_space/colab/rs07_coherence.py#L1-L5), [rs07_coherence.py](records_space/colab/rs07_coherence.py#L13-L37)

**Label structure** (`rs03_run.py` diagnostics b/c) measures k=15 purity for twelve labels (protein, c30 homology cluster, paper, source, NA class, temperature state, pool, phase-separation label, morphology, csat link, buffer family, readout class), always reporting the chance level `(Σp²)` alongside. The sharpest result: a neighbour-vote AUROC on the phase-separation label reaches **0.84 when neighbours from the same paper are allowed** (shared lab conventions make records comparable), but collapses to **0.50 with protein similarity** and **0.59 with conditions only** across papers and proteins — the README quotes these numbers as an explicit warning that the map is not a phase-separation predictor.

Sources: [rs03_run.py](records_space/colab/rs03_run.py#L132-L181), [README.md](records_space/README.md#L31-L31), [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L359-L397)

**Projection fidelity and coverage**: `neighbor_overlap` checks how many high-dimensional k=15 neighbours survive into each 2-D embedding; the missingness analysis counts distinct missing-dimension patterns and their within-paper agreement versus chance; and a csat-coverage diagnostic measures how far csat records fall inside the 15-NN radius of binary records, per NA class. These outputs (`diagnostics.json`, `knn_<lens>.npz`) are the audit trail of every lens.

Sources: [rs03_run.py](records_space/colab/rs03_run.py#L183-L226), [rslib.py](records_space/colab/rslib.py#L388-L397), [rs03_run.py](records_space/colab/rs03_run.py#L77-L84)

## Module Architecture: Offline Engine versus Browser Mirror

The distance model exists twice by design — once where data is private and compute is free (Colab), once where the user's sequence must never leave the page. `rs09_export_explorer_data.py` is the bridge: it serializes the scaled model inputs as typed arrays (`records.bin`, `seqs.bin` with layout manifests in JSON), dumps every scale and normalization constant into `params.json`, and trains the approximation model.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph offline["Offline — Colab / Python"]
        TSV["rs_records.tsv · rs_sequences.tsv<br/>esmc_L18.npy"] --> RSLIB["rslib.py<br/>build_inputs · calibrate_P<br/>compute_lens_matrices"]
        RSLIB --> DIAG["knn_*.npz · diagnostics.json<br/>rs_coords.tsv"]
        RSLIB --> EXP["rs09 export<br/>params.json · records.bin · seqs.bin<br/>approx.json · coverage.json"]
    end
    EXP --> SPACE
    subgraph browser["Browser — records_space.js"]
        SPACE["Space class<br/>typed-array views of .bin files"]
        SPACE --> DIST["distances(q)<br/>four lenses, λ, temp penalty"]
        SPACE --> APPROX["approxZ()<br/>Ridge: comp24+dimer → Zn"]
        APPROX --> DIST
    end
    DIAG --> PAGE["explorer index.html<br/>(precomputed coordinates)"]
    DIST --> TRY["Try-panel: nearest records,<br/>coverage, honest disclosure"]
```

Sources: [rs09_export_explorer_data.py](records_space/colab/rs09_export_explorer_data.py#L2-L10), [records_space.js](records_space/explorer/js/records_space.js#L62-L71)

## The Browser Reimplementation

The `Space.distances(q)` method is a line-for-line port of the Python block functions: the same five-dimension condition mean, the same salt/crowder group truncation, the same λ rule, the same present-vs-none N-block rule, and the same four lens formulas. `buildQuery` converts the parsed condition fields into the exact scaled space using the exported scales (`x / s` for range-scaled, `log10(1+x) / s` for salts and crowders, z-scored NA features divided by the q95 calibration), so a query constructed in JavaScript lands in the identical geometry as the precomputed records.

Sources: [records_space.js](records_space/explorer/js/records_space.js#L106-L160), [records_space.js](records_space/explorer/js/records_space.js#L169-L196), [params.json](records_space/export/params.json#L10-L30)

**Sequence identity handling** decides which P-block input a pasted sequence gets. Every dataset sequence is fingerprinted offline with two FNV-1a 32-bit whole-sequence hashes plus a FracMinHash sketch of 5-mers (keeping hashes below 2³²/8). In the browser, `analyzeSequence` classifies the input: `exact` (hash + length match → the true stored `Zn` is used), `variant` (containment ≥ 0.5 or Jaccard ≥ 0.3), `related`, or `novel` — and only novel sequences fall through to the approximation model. This is also a privacy mechanism: the page stores sketches, never raw sequences, and all matching happens in-page.

Sources: [rs09_export_explorer_data.py](records_space/colab/rs09_export_explorer_data.py#L25-L48), [records_space.js](records_space/explorer/js/records_space.js#L28-L32), [records_space.js](records_space/explorer/js/records_space.js#L75-L95)

## Approximate Embeddings for Novel Sequences

A novel sequence cannot get a real ESMC embedding in a browser, so `rs09` trains a **ridge regression from sequence composition to embedding space**: features are `comp24` (24 dimensions — log length, 20 amino-acid frequencies, charge, acidic/basic, aromatic fractions) concatenated with `dimer400` (400 normalized dipeptide frequencies), giving the 424-feature model exported in `approx.json` with `alpha = 100.0`. Its output is L2-normalized in the browser (`approxZ`) and substituted for `Zn` in the P block.

Model selection is the interesting part: five alphas are evaluated with **GroupKFold(5) grouped by c30 homology clusters**, and the winner is chosen by mean **top-15 neighbour overlap** between approximate and true cosine similarities — optimizing exactly the quantity the Try-panel depends on (neighbourhoods, not pointwise accuracy). The trained model is then re-fit on all sequences and exported as `W (424×64)`, intercept, and feature mean/std.

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Features | comp24 (24) + dimer400 (400) = 424, standardized |
| Model | Ridge regression, α = 100 → 64-d Zn, L2-normalized |
| Validation | GroupKFold(5) by c30 cluster; metric = top-15 neighbour overlap + cosine(Ẑ, Z) |
| User contract | the page explicitly states the embedding is approximate and shows nearest records + neighbourhood coverage |

Sources: [approx.json](records_space/export/approx.json#L1-L1), [rs09_export_explorer_data.py](records_space/colab/rs09_export_explorer_data.py#L120-L163), [records_space.js](records_space/explorer/js/records_space.js#L96-L104), [README.md](records_space/README.md#L32-L32)

> [!TIP]
> Grouping the cross-validation folds by c30 homology cluster is what makes the overlap metric trustworthy: ungrouped folds would let near-identical sequences leak between train and test, inflating the neighbour-overlap score for a model that in reality must generalize across protein families.

## End-to-End Data Flow

The full path from raw tables to the interactive page runs through five numbered stages, each a standalone script so results can be cached and re-run selectively (`rs03 → knn/coords/diagnostics → rs09 → export → rs05` builds the final single-file `index.html`).

| Stage | Script | Consumes | Produces |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Embeddings | `rs02_embed_new_seqs.py` | csat-only sequences | `esmc_L18_new.npy` |
| 2. Distances + maps | `rs03_run.py` | records, sequences, embeddings | 4 lens matrices, UMAP/t-SNE coords, `diagnostics.json`, `knn_*.npz` |
| 3. Coherence | `rs07_coherence.py` | `knn_*.npz` | `diagnostics_coherence.json` |
| 4. Export | `rs09_export_explorer_data.py` | everything above | `params.json`, `records.bin`, `seqs.bin`, `approx.json`, coverage |
| 5. Build page | `scripts/rs05_build_explorer.py` | export + template | self-contained `records_space/index.html` |

Sources: [rs03_run.py](records_space/colab/rs03_run.py#L1-L10), [rs09_export_explorer_data.py](records_space/colab/rs09_export_explorer_data.py#L164-L200), [README.md](records_space/README.md#L58-L66)

## Where to Go Next

To see the distance model from a user's perspective — lens switching, colouring, and the Try-panel workflow — continue with [Interactive Explorer Tour](4-interactive-explorer-tour). The embedding that powers the P block is documented in [Protein and Nucleic Acid Embeddings](12-protein-and-nucleic-acid-embeddings). The hollow-ring protein universe that extends the same ESMC/UMAP machinery to 6,338 unlabelled proteins is covered in [Negatives and Protein Universe](20-negatives-and-protein-universe), and the scripts that assemble the final site in [Site Build Pipeline](21-site-build-pipeline). For the export parameters consumed by the page, the full grid lives in [Hyperparameter Grid Reference](22-hyperparameter-grid-reference).

# Negatives and Protein Universe



This page documents two closely related artifacts of the Records Space subsystem. The first is the **"LLPS negatives and unlabelled proteins" page** (`records_space/negatives/index.html`) — an interactive map of every protein used as a *training negative* by published LLPS predictors, placed against an unlabelled Swiss-Prot reference background in a shared ESMC-600M embedding space. The second is the **protein universe** (`explorer/universe_data.json`) — the extension of the Records Space to proteins mentioned by the tools but absent from the OpenPhase record tables. Both artifacts share one embedding contract and one build philosophy: heavy GPU work runs on ephemeral Colab sessions, while all assembly is done locally with pure-stdlib scripts so no numpy dependency is needed on the build machine.

Sources: [rs14_pu_manifest.py](records_space/scripts/rs14_pu_manifest.py#L1-L7), [rs16_build_pu.py](records_space/scripts/rs16_build_pu.py#L1-L4), [rs13_universe_export.py](records_space/scripts/rs13_universe_export.py#L1-L4)

## Why Negatives and Unlabelled Deserve Their Own Map

The negative sets in LLPS research are epistemically fragile: a "negative" is almost always a protein that a tool's training corpus simply *does not list* as phase-separating, not a protein experimentally shown not to phase-separate. The page states this caveat directly in its highlight note — "Negative sets are mostly proteins that were not listed as phase-separating, so many may be unlabelled rather than shown not to phase-separate" — and its subtitle frames the whole map as "the training negatives of ten tools and PPMC, and a Swiss-Prot reference sample as the unlabelled background. Positives are not shown." Every protein on the page therefore carries exactly one of two roles: **N** (negative in at least one tool) or **U** (unlabelled Swiss-Prot reference).

Sources: [negatives_template.html](records_space/home_page/negatives_template.html#L244), [negatives_template.html](records_space/home_page/negatives_template.html#L149)

## The Set Registry and the PU Manifest

Everything on the page is derived from one flat manifest, `pu_manifest.tsv`, produced by `rs14_pu_manifest.py`. The script assembles a registry of up to 32 sets, each owning a single bit in a per-protein bitmask:

- **12 negative sets** (these get real bits on the page): PPMC's NP (non-phase-separating, protein-level) and ND (non-phase-separating, disordered) classes, plus the training negatives of ten tools (catGRANULE 2.0, FuzDrop, LLPhyScore, LLPS-predict, OptPredLLPS, PPT-taskA, ProtGPS, PSAP, PScalpel, PSPHunter, PSPire).
- **11 positive sets** (tool training positives, PPMC DE/CE/C_D, LTP, HTP) that receive bits in the working mask but are *stripped before export* — they exist solely to veto proteins from being counted as "unlabelled".
- **A Swiss-Prot background** of 16,000 sequences (12,000 random + 4,000 human, 50–1,000 aa) reused from the world-and-cluster-maps project with precomputed layer-18 embeddings.

The core selection rule is `mask & N_BITS`: a protein with any negative-set bit becomes role `N` (even if it is a positive elsewhere — the page deliberately does not mark that), while a background protein with an all-zero negative mask becomes `U`. Proteins that appear *only* in positive sets never enter the manifest.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph registry["rs14 set registry (≤ 32 bits)"]
    P["11 positive sets<br/>tool training positives · PPMC DE/CE/C_D · LTP · HTP"]
    N["12 negative sets<br/>10 tool training negatives · PPMC NP / ND"]
    BG["Swiss-Prot background<br/>16,000 seqs · ESMC L18 precomputed"]
  end
  P -- "bits erased — used only as a veto" --> M["per-protein mask (uint32)"]
  N -- "bits kept" --> M
  M -- "mask ≠ 0" --> RN["role = N<br/>negative in ≥ 1 tool"]
  M -- "mask = 0 ∧ in background" --> RU["role = U<br/>unlabelled reference"]
```

Each manifest row also records the **embedding source** for the protein, with strict priority `uni` (protein-universe Colab shards) > `bg` (Swiss-Prot reference matrix) > `seqs` (PPMC full-length sequence table) > `new` (must be fetched and embedded on Colab). IDs with no source are written to `pu_new_ids.tsv`, the exact input format rs15 expects.

Sources: [rs14_pu_manifest.py](records_space/scripts/rs14_pu_manifest.py#L27-L67), [rs14_pu_manifest.py](records_space/scripts/rs14_pu_manifest.py#L84-L90), [rs14_pu_manifest.py](records_space/scripts/rs14_pu_manifest.py#L103-L115), [rs14_pu_manifest.py](records_space/scripts/rs14_pu_manifest.py#L1-L7)

> [!TIP]
> Positive sets are excluded from the exported mask (`mask & N_BITS` in rs14 L89) but still computed — this is what prevents a known driver like FUS from silently counting as "unlabelled" in the U layer. Any consumer of `pu_manifest.tsv` inherits this veto for free; consumers of the final page payload do not, since only negative bits survive.

## From Manifest to Map: the PU Pipeline

The pipeline splits cleanly along the GPU boundary. Colab scripts (`rs12`, `rs15`) handle sequence fetching and embedding; local stdlib scripts (`rs13`, `rs16`, `rs17`) handle assembly and page generation. Orchestration shell scripts request an A100 → L4 → T4 session in fallback order, upload inputs, launch the driver remotely, and mirror output shards back until an `ALL_DONE` sentinel appears.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph local["Local machine — pure stdlib"]
    RS14["rs14_pu_manifest.py<br/>pu_manifest.tsv · sets.json · pu_new_ids.tsv"]
    RS13E["rs13_universe_export.py<br/>explorer/universe_data.json"]
    RS16["rs16_build_pu.py<br/>pu_page/index.html + page_fragment.html + summary.json"]
    RS17["rs17_build_site.py<br/>site/records_space/negatives/index.html"]
  end
  subgraph gpu["Ephemeral Colab GPU session"]
    RS12["rs12_universe.py<br/>universe: fetch → ESMC-600M L18 → shards"]
    RS15["rs15_pu.py<br/>new proteins → embed → PCA(64) → UMAP(cosine)"]
    RUNPU["run_pu.sh<br/>uploads manifest + bg/seqs embeddings + uni shards"]
    RUNUNI["run_universe.sh<br/>uploads universe_ids + rs_sequences + L18 matrices"]
    RUNUNI --> RS12
    RUNPU --> RS15
    RS12 -- "universe.npz → emb_shard_*.npz" --> RS13E
    RS15 -- "pu_map.npz" --> RS16
  end
  RS14 -. "pu_new_ids.tsv" .-> RUNPU
  RS12 -. "emb_shard_*.npz reused as uni source" .-> RUNPU
  RS16 --> RS17
```

Both runners persist reusable state: `run_pu.sh` accepts a `RESUME_DIR` whose `emb_shard_*.npz` and `universe.fasta` are pre-uploaded so reruns skip sequence fetching and embedding entirely, and `run_universe.sh` mirrors shard files continuously rather than waiting for job completion.

Sources: [run_pu.sh](records_space/colab/run_pu.sh#L2-L9), [run_pu.sh](records_space/colab/run_pu.sh#L29-L37), [run_universe.sh](records_space/colab/run_universe.sh#L2-L17), [run_universe.sh](records_space/colab/run_universe.sh#L36-L38), [rs17_build_site.py](records_space/scripts/rs17_build_site.py#L94-L97)

## One Embedding Contract, Two Fits

Both scripts honor the same embedding contract established elsewhere in the repository (see [Protein and Nucleic Acid Embeddings](12-protein-and-nucleic-acid-embeddings)): ESMC-600M **layer 18** (hidden-states index), **residue mean** pooling that excludes special tokens and padding. rs12 fixes the constants `LAYER=18, MAXLEN=2000, TOKEN_BUDGET=14000, SHARD=1500`, and its docstring states the reference statistics precisely: `e_mu/e_sd` are the per-dimension mean and standard deviation of the dataset's 1,338 sequences, with PCA(64) fitted on those same dataset embeddings before L2 normalization.

rs15 reuses rs12's fetch and embed functions but **re-fits its own projection** on the assembled PU matrix: z-score the pooled embeddings, `PCA(n_components=64, random_state=0)`, recentre, L2-normalize, then `UMAP(n_neighbors=30, min_dist=0.25, metric="cosine", random_state=0)`. Proteins whose embedding cannot be assembled from any of the four sources are dropped (with a logged count), and a NaN assert guards the matrix before projection.

| Aspect | rs12 (protein universe) | rs15 (negatives/unlabelled page) |
|---|---|---|
| Input proteins | Tool-mentioned IDs not in the records space | All `pu_manifest.tsv` rows |
| Sequence fetch | Batch-of-100 UniProt + per-ID UniParc fallback | Same functions via `R12.fetch_all` |
| Embedding sources | Dataset L18 matrices + fresh shards | `uni` / `bg` / `seqs` / `new` by manifest priority |
| PCA fit | On the dataset's 1,338 sequence embeddings | On the assembled PU matrix itself |
| UMAP input | Universe + dataset sequences jointly | PU proteins only |
| Output | `universe.npz`, `universe.fasta`, `universe_meta.tsv`, shards | `pu_map.npz`, `pu_new_meta.tsv`, `missing_ids.txt` |

Sources: [rs12_universe.py](records_space/colab/rs12_universe.py#L1-L10), [rs12_universe.py](records_space/colab/rs12_universe.py#L22), [rs12_universe.py](records_space/colab/rs12_universe.py#L85-L133), [rs15_pu.py](records_space/colab/rs15_pu.py#L39-L47), [rs15_pu.py](records_space/colab/rs15_pu.py#L57-L77)

> [!TIP]
> Because rs15 fits its own PCA/UMAP on the PU proteins while rs12 projects the universe through dataset-fitted statistics, **coordinates from the two artifacts are not comparable**. Never copy `pu_map.npz` coordinates into a universe-space view or vice versa; each JSON carries its own normalized coordinate frame.

## Page Payload: Typed-Array Encoding

`rs16_build_pu.py` merges `pu_map.npz` coordinates with the manifest and `sets.json` into a single inline JSON blob injected at the template's `/*__DATA__*/null` placeholder. Numeric columns are base64-encoded little-endian typed arrays to keep the standalone HTML small: coordinates as `Uint16` quantized to `[0, 65535]` with a 4% margin and a **Y-axis flip** (canvas origin top-left), role/flag as `Uint8`, the negative-set mask as `Uint32`, and sequence length as `Uint16`. The decoder in the page reconstructs them with `atob` + `Uint16Array`/`Uint32Array` views and computes per-protein set counts with a bitwise population-count routine.

The `flag` byte packs three orthogonal facts per protein:

| Bit (value) | Meaning | Rendered as |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | In the Swiss-Prot reference sample | "Reference" field in the card |
| 2 | Also has records with conditions in the Records space | Dark ring around the dot |
| 4 | Obsolete UniProtKB entry; sequence recovered from UniParc | "No longer in UniProtKB" note |

Set sizes are recomputed at build time (`nn` per set) and the **top-6 pairwise overlaps** between negative sets are emitted as `pairs` — the page's overview card renders the top four, e.g. 11,264 proteins negative in both LLPS-predict and PSAP training sets, 7,665 shared between PSAP and PSPire. rs16 also asserts every exported set has `role == "N"`, structurally guaranteeing the page stays positives-free, and writes a machine-readable `summary.json` (role counts, in-records count, obsolete count, k-set histogram, multi-set percentage, new-embedded and missing-ID counts).

Sources: [rs16_build_pu.py](records_space/scripts/rs16_build_pu.py#L38-L54), [rs16_build_pu.py](records_space/scripts/rs16_build_pu.py#L55-L74), [rs16_build_pu.py](records_space/scripts/rs16_build_pu.py#L75-L91), [negatives_template.html](records_space/home_page/negatives_template.html#L131), [negatives_template.html](records_space/home_page/negatives_template.html#L137-L142), [negatives_template.html](records_space/home_page/negatives_template.html#L252-L257)

## Reading the Interactive Map

The page is a self-contained canvas application — rail (controls) | square stage | card — with no framework dependencies. Its controls map directly onto the payload:

- **Layer toggles** show/hide roles U and N with live counts.
- **Find protein** searches accession prefix, exact gene, or name substring (max 8 hits) and re-pins the map even if the target's layer was hidden.
- **Highlight a negative set** dims everything to 55% opacity and enlarges the selected set's members to 1.9× radius in the source's brand color; the note re-states the absence-of-evidence caveat for that set.
- **Colour negatives by count** bins proteins into 1 / 2 / 3 / 4-or-more set memberships using the palette `--n1…--n4`.
- **Density** renders a Gaussian-smoothed glow (192×192 grid, radius-7 kernel, σ=2.4, normalized to the 99.5th percentile) under the points for negatives, unlabelled, or both — making it easy to see whether tool negatives occupy the same embedding regions as the unlabelled background.
- **Protein card** shows UniProt accession (linking to uniprot.org), gene, organism, length, reference membership, obsolete status, and the list of sets naming this protein as negative; the overview card exposes the totals, overlap pairs, and the background-sample explanation.

Sources: [negatives/index.html](records_space/negatives/index.html#L114-L131), [negatives_template.html](records_space/home_page/negatives_template.html#L179-L198), [negatives_template.html](records_space/home_page/negatives_template.html#L219-L228), [negatives_template.html](records_space/home_page/negatives_template.html#L261-L266), [negatives_template.html](records_space/home_page/negatives_template.html#L269-L282), [negatives_template.html](records_space/home_page/negatives_template.html#L313-L314)

## The Protein Universe Artifact for the Explorer

The parallel artifact, `explorer/universe_data.json`, is produced by `rs13_universe_export.py` from rs12's `universe.npz`. Because the build machine has no numpy, rs13 implements a **stdlib `.npy`/`.npz` reader** (zipfile + struct) supporting float16/32/64, integers, booleans, and fixed-width Unicode strings — the same `load_npz` helper that rs16 imports for `pu_map.npz`. The exported fields:

| Field | Encoding | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `xy`, `xyds` | base64 `Uint16` pairs | UMAP coordinates, normalized to `[0,1]` with 4% margin (universe proteins and dataset sequences through one shared frame) |
| `zn` | base64 `int8` | Projected z-coordinate, scaled ×127 and clamped to ±127 |
| `nn`, `nncos` | int arrays | Nearest dataset-sequence index and its cosine similarity (×100) |
| `trunc`, `obs` | 0/1 arrays | Truncated-sequence flag; obsolete-UniProtKB (UniParc-sourced) flag |
| `lo`, `hi` | base64 `Uint32` pair | 64-bit set-membership mask split into two words |
| `acc/name/gene/len/org/missing` | plain JSON | Metadata, with names truncated to 56 chars, plus the missing-ID count |

This JSON is what powers the universe overlay described in the [Interactive Explorer Tour](4-interactive-explorer-tour); it answers, for every tool-mentioned protein outside the records, "where does it sit relative to our 1,338 sequences, and which one is it closest to?"

Sources: [rs13_universe_export.py](records_space/scripts/rs13_universe_export.py#L1-L4), [rs13_universe_export.py](records_space/scripts/rs13_universe_export.py#L19-L46), [rs13_universe_export.py](records_space/scripts/rs13_universe_export.py#L56-L88)

## Regeneration Playbook
